questions.stem: A host is configured with 172.16.20.75/26. Which address is the broadcast address of the subnet the host belongs to?

explanation.correct: A /26 is a 255.255.255.192 mask, so subnets step by 64 in the 4th octet: .0, .64, .128, .192. The host .75 falls in the .64 subnet (range .64–.127); the broadcast is the last address, .127.

distractors.A: 172.16.20.63 is the broadcast of the .0 subnet, one block too low.
distractors.B: 172.16.20.64 is the network (subnet) address of this block, not the broadcast.
distractors.D: 172.16.20.128 is the next subnet's network address.

explanation.exam_pattern: Find the block size (256 − mask octet = 256 − 192 = 64), list the subnet boundaries, then the broadcast is one less than the next boundary.

questions.stem: You need subnets with at least 50 usable hosts each, using the fewest host bits. Enter the prefix length (e.g. 24) you would use.

explanation.correct: 6 host bits give 2^6 − 2 = 62 usable hosts (≥50); 5 host bits give only 30. 32 − 6 = /26.
explanation.exam_pattern: Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2. Find the smallest host-bit count that still covers the requirement, then prefix = 32 − host bits.

questions.stem: Which statement about the IPv6 address 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:00AB:0000:1234 and its correct compressed form is true?

explanation.correct: Leading zeros in each hextet are dropped and the single longest run of all-zero hextets is replaced by one ::. That collapses the three 0000 hextets to ::, giving 2001:DB8::AB:0:1234.

distractors.B: :: may appear only ONCE in an address; two :: is ambiguous and invalid.
distractors.C: This still shows the zero hextets explicitly AND a :: — you cannot mix the two for the same run.
distractors.D: 2001 was wrongly shortened to 21; you remove leading zeros per hextet, not digits across the address.

explanation.exam_pattern: Only one :: allowed, and it replaces the LONGEST zero run. Watch for answers with two :: or with digits (not leading zeros) removed.

questions.stem: An interface has MAC address 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E and derives its interface ID with EUI-64. What is the resulting 64-bit interface ID?

explanation.correct: EUI-64 inserts FFFE in the middle of the MAC and flips the 7th bit (U/L bit) of the first byte. 00 (0000 0000) becomes 02 (0000 0010), then 001A2B + FFFE + 3C4D5E → 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E.

distractors.B: The U/L bit was not flipped; 00 must become 02.
distractors.C: The inserted value must be FFFE, not FFFE split as FE/FF, and the 7th bit flip is on the first byte only.
distractors.D: FFFF was inserted instead of FFFE.

explanation.exam_pattern: EUI-64 = split MAC, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit of byte 1. The flip usually turns 00→02; answers that skip the flip are traps.

questions.stem: Which TWO protocols/applications rely on UDP for transport by default?

explanation.correct: TFTP (UDP/69) and SNMP (UDP/161,162) are UDP-based — lightweight, no connection setup. FTP, HTTP and Telnet all use TCP for reliability.

distractors.B: HTTP uses TCP/80 — reliable, ordered delivery for web traffic.
distractors.D: FTP uses TCP/21 (control) and TCP/20 (data).

explanation.exam_pattern: Remember the small UDP club: DNS(53 usually), DHCP(67/68), TFTP(69), SNMP(161/162), NTP(123), syslog(514), plus voice/video (RTP).

questions.stem: A frame arrives on a switch for a destination MAC that is NOT in the MAC address table. What does the switch do?

options.text: Drops the frame and sends an ICMP unreachable
Floods the frame out all ports in the VLAN except the ingress port
Floods the frame out every port including the ingress port
Forwards the frame to the default gateway

explanation.correct: An unknown unicast is flooded out all ports in the same VLAN except the port it arrived on. When the real host replies, the switch learns its MAC and future frames are forwarded, not flooded.

distractors.A: Switches do not generate ICMP for Layer 2 forwarding; that is a router behaviour.
distractors.C: The ingress port is always excluded from flooding (split-horizon of flooding).
distractors.D: Layer 2 switches do not consult a gateway; that is Layer 3 routing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast are flooded within the VLAN, never out the ingress port. Learning is based on SOURCE MAC.

questions.stem: As data is encapsulated for transmission, in which order are the PDUs created moving DOWN the TCP/IP stack from the application?

explanation.correct: Transport adds the L4 header (Segment), the network layer adds the IP header (Packet), the data-link layer adds the frame header/trailer (Frame), and the physical layer transmits Bits.

distractors.B: Segmentation (L4) happens before the packet (L3) header is added.
distractors.C: This is reversed — framing is not first on the way down.
distractors.D: This is the de-encapsulation (receive) order, moving up the stack.

explanation.exam_pattern: Down the stack = Segment, Packet, Frame, Bits (SPFB). Up the stack reverses it. Watch whether the question asks about sending or receiving.

questions.stem: You are directly connecting two Cisco switches that do NOT support Auto-MDIX. Which cable is required between their FastEthernet ports?

options.text: Crossover (568B on one end, 568A on the other)

explanation.correct: Switch-to-switch is a 'like device' connection, which requires a crossover cable when Auto-MDIX is unavailable, so TX on one side maps to RX on the other.

distractors.A: Straight-through is for unlike devices (switch↔router, switch↔PC).
distractors.C: Rollover cables connect a PC's serial/USB to a device console port.
distractors.D: Coax is not used for modern switched Ethernet access links.

explanation.exam_pattern: Like devices (switch-switch, router-router, PC-PC, PC-router) → crossover. Unlike devices → straight-through. Auto-MDIX makes it moot if enabled.

questions.stem: Four switches run Rapid-PVST+ for VLAN 10. Their VLAN 10 bridge priorities and MAC addresses are shown. Which switch becomes the root bridge?
questions.exhibit:
SW-A  priority 32768  MAC 0012.3f00.aa00
SW-B  priority 32768  MAC 0012.3f00.0b00
SW-C  priority 24576  MAC 0012.3f00.cc00
SW-D  priority 28672  MAC 0012.3f00.0d00

explanation.correct: The root is the lowest Bridge ID = priority (incl. the VLAN sys-id-ext) THEN MAC as tiebreaker. SW-C has the lowest priority (24576), so it wins outright — MAC is never consulted because priority already decides it.

distractors.A: SW-A uses the default 32768, higher than SW-C and SW-D.
distractors.B: Lowest MAC only breaks a tie when priorities are EQUAL. SW-C's lower priority settles it before MAC matters.
distractors.D: SW-D's 28672 is lower than the defaults but still higher than SW-C's 24576.

explanation.exam_pattern: Compare priority FIRST (lower wins); only if two match do you fall to the lower MAC. The classic trap dangles a tiny MAC to lure you past a lower-priority switch.

questions.stem: You run 'spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary' on a switch where the current root has priority 32769 (32768 + VLAN 1). What priority does the local switch set for VLAN 1?

explanation.correct: The 'root primary' macro sets priority to 24576 when the existing root's priority is greater than 24576. (If the current root were already ≤24576, it would instead set 4096 below that root.)

distractors.A: 0 is a valid manual priority but not what the macro chooses here.
distractors.B: 4096 is the step size and what 'root primary' would pick only if the current root were already at/below 24576.
distractors.D: 28672 is what 'root secondary' configures.

explanation.exam_pattern: root primary → 24576 (or 4096 under the current root if it's already low). root secondary → 28672. These are macros, not fixed priorities.

questions.stem: SW1 ports are set to 'channel-group 1 mode desirable'. SW2's matching ports are set to 'channel-group 1 mode auto'. What is the result?

options.text: The channel does not form; both sides are passive
The channel does not form; mismatched protocols

explanation.correct: desirable and auto are PAgP modes. desirable actively initiates PAgP; auto responds but does not initiate. desirable/auto forms a PAgP channel because at least one side (desirable) initiates.

distractors.A: LACP uses active/passive, not desirable/auto. desirable/auto is PAgP.
distractors.C: auto/auto would fail (neither initiates), but desirable DOES initiate.
distractors.D: Both sides are PAgP here, so there is no protocol mismatch.

explanation.exam_pattern: PAgP = desirable/auto; LACP = active/passive. The only non-forming same-protocol combos are auto/auto and passive/passive (nobody initiates). 'on' only works with 'on'.

questions.stem: Which EtherChannel mode combination will FAIL to form a bundle?

explanation.correct: passive/passive fails because LACP passive only responds to LACP packets — neither side sends the first LACP frame, so negotiation never starts.

distractors.A: active/passive works: active initiates, passive responds.
distractors.B: active/active works: both initiate LACP.
distractors.D: on/on forms a static channel with no negotiation at all.

explanation.exam_pattern: The two 'dead' pairs are passive/passive (LACP) and auto/auto (PAgP). Also remember 'on' must pair only with 'on' — on/active or on/desirable fail.

questions.stem: A trunk between SW1 (native VLAN 1) and SW2 (native VLAN 99) logs %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Traffic in the native VLAN of each switch can leak between VLANs 1 and 99
The trunk is administratively shut down automatically
All tagged VLAN traffic stops crossing the trunk
The mismatch has no effect because native VLAN traffic is tagged

explanation.correct: Each switch sends its native VLAN untagged and assumes untagged frames belong to its own native VLAN. With a mismatch, SW1's VLAN 1 untagged frames land in SW2's VLAN 99 — a security/bridging problem (VLAN hopping risk).

distractors.B: The trunk stays up; only a log message is generated (CDP detects it).
distractors.C: Tagged VLANs still cross fine; only the untagged native VLAN is affected.
distractors.D: The native VLAN is UNtagged by default — that is exactly why the mismatch matters.

explanation.exam_pattern: Native VLAN mismatch = untagged frames cross into the wrong VLAN, flagged by CDP, trunk stays up. Fix by matching native VLANs on both ends.

questions.stem: Two switches both default their ports to 'switchport mode dynamic auto'. What will the link between them become?

options.text: An 802.1Q trunk only if encapsulation is set to negotiate

explanation.correct: dynamic auto only trunks if the other side actively asks (dynamic desirable or trunk). auto/auto means neither side initiates DTP, so the link stays an access port in VLAN 1.

distractors.A: DTP needs at least one 'desirable' or 'trunk' side to form a trunk; auto/auto does not negotiate up.
distractors.C: Encapsulation choice is irrelevant when no trunk is negotiated at all.
distractors.D: Switchports do not auto-become routed ports; that requires 'no switchport'.

explanation.exam_pattern: DTP table: auto/auto and (auto or access)/access stay access; desirable or trunk on one side pulls auto up to a trunk. Best practice is to hard-set mode and 'switchport nonegotiate'.

questions.stem: On a non-root switch running Rapid-PVST+, which port role is placed in the forwarding state and is the single best path toward the root bridge?

explanation.correct: The root port is the one port on a non-root bridge with the lowest cost to the root; it forwards and is the upstream path to the root.

distractors.A: Designated ports forward too, but they face AWAY from the root on each segment (one per segment), not toward it.
distractors.C: An alternate port is a blocked backup to the ROOT port (an alternate path to the root); it does not forward unless the root port fails.
distractors.D: A backup port is a blocked backup for a DESIGNATED port on the same segment (seen with hubs); it does not forward.

explanation.exam_pattern: Root port = best path TOWARD root (one per non-root switch). Designated = best path on a segment AWAY from root. Alternate/Backup = blocked (RSTP terms).

questions.stem: In a split-MAC (lightweight AP + WLC) deployment, which protocol tunnels both control and data traffic between a lightweight AP and the WLC?

explanation.correct: CAPWAP builds two tunnels between the AP and WLC: a control tunnel (UDP 5246, encrypted via DTLS) and a data tunnel (UDP 5247). It is the modern standard that replaced the older LWAPP.

distractors.B: LWAPP is the legacy predecessor; CAPWAP superseded it (RFC 5415).
distractors.C: GRE is not the AP-to-WLC tunneling protocol in split-MAC designs.
distractors.D: 802.1Q is VLAN tagging on wired trunks, not an AP-to-WLC tunnel.

explanation.exam_pattern: CAPWAP ports: 5246 control (DTLS encrypted), 5247 data. Split-MAC means the AP does real-time 802.11, the WLC does management/auth.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish LLDP from CDP?

options.text: LLDP is an IEEE (802.1AB) open standard; CDP is Cisco-proprietary
CDP is enabled globally by default on Cisco devices; LLDP is disabled by default
CDP uses TCP port 179 to exchange information

explanation.correct: LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) is vendor-neutral, useful in multivendor networks; CDP is Cisco-proprietary and is ON by default, while LLDP must be enabled with 'lldp run'.

distractors.C: LLDP's whole purpose is multivendor discovery — it DOES see non-Cisco devices.
distractors.D: Both CDP and LLDP are Layer 2 protocols; they do not use TCP/179 (that's BGP).

explanation.exam_pattern: CDP = Cisco, on by default, L2. LLDP = open standard (802.1AB), off by default ('lldp run'), L2. Default CDP timers: 60s hello, 180s hold.

questions.stem: On interface Gi0/1 you must allow ONLY VLANs 10, 20, and 30 across the trunk (replacing the default allowed list). Enter the exact interface command.

explanation.correct: 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30' sets the allowed list to exactly those VLANs. Use the 'add' keyword later to append without overwriting the list.
explanation.exam_pattern: Without 'add', the command REPLACES the whole allowed list — a classic outage trap when you forget 'add' and knock off every other VLAN.

questions.stem: Two OSPF routers on an Ethernet segment are stuck with their neighbor in the 2-WAY state and never reach FULL. Which explanation is MOST likely correct?

options.text: This is normal between two DROTHER routers on a broadcast segment
There is an OSPF area mismatch on the link
The MTU values do not match on the two interfaces
The OSPF process IDs do not match between the routers

explanation.correct: On a broadcast network, DROTHER routers intentionally stay in 2-WAY with each other — they only go FULL with the DR and BDR. 2-WAY between two DROTHERs is expected, not a fault.

distractors.B: An area mismatch prevents the adjacency from forming at all (stuck in INIT/EXSTART or no neighbor), not a clean 2-WAY.
distractors.C: An MTU mismatch sticks the neighbor in EXSTART/EXCHANGE, not 2-WAY.
distractors.D: OSPF process IDs are locally significant and do NOT need to match between neighbors.

explanation.exam_pattern: Map the stuck state to the cause: INIT=one-way hello; 2-WAY=normal DROTHER-DROTHER; EXSTART/EXCHANGE=MTU mismatch; stuck forming=hello/dead, area, subnet, or auth mismatch.

questions.stem: Review the output. Why is the OSPF adjacency not reaching FULL?
questions.exhibit:
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri   State      Dead Time   Address      Interface
10.1.1.1          1   EXSTART/DR 00:00:33    10.0.12.1    GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The routers have mismatched OSPF hello/dead timers
The interface MTU differs between the two routers
The two routers are in different OSPF areas

explanation.correct: A neighbor stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE that never advances to FULL is the textbook symptom of an MTU mismatch: the DBD packets are exchanged but the larger-MTU side's DBD is dropped, so the exchange loops.

distractors.A: Mismatched hello/dead timers stop the neighbor from forming at all — you would not even see it reach EXSTART.
distractors.C: An area mismatch likewise prevents neighborship; the neighbor would not appear.
distractors.D: Auth mismatch prevents the adjacency from forming (no neighbor), not an EXSTART hang.

explanation.exam_pattern: EXSTART/EXCHANGE + 'stuck' = MTU mismatch. Verify with 'show ip ospf interface' (look at the MTU) and fix with 'mtu'/'ip mtu' or 'ip ospf mtu-ignore' as a workaround.

questions.stem: You must write a single OSPF network statement that matches ONLY the subnet 192.168.8.0/22 (the whole /22). Enter the wildcard mask to use after 'network 192.168.8.0'.

explanation.exam_pattern: Wildcard = inverse of the subnet mask (255 − each octet). /22 → 252 in the 3rd octet → wildcard 3 there. The trap is writing 0.0.255.255 (/16) or 0.0.0.255 (/24) instead of 0.0.3.255.

questions.stem: Which wildcard mask, used with 'access-list 10 permit 10.1.0.0 <wildcard>', matches every host in 10.1.0.0 through 10.1.3.255 and NO other addresses?

explanation.correct: 10.1.0.0–10.1.3.255 is a /22 (four /24 blocks: .0,.1,.2,.3). The /22 wildcard is 0.0.3.255 — the low two bits of the third octet are 'don't care'.

distractors.D: 255.255.252.0 is a subnet MASK, not a wildcard — it is backwards.

explanation.exam_pattern: Range size 4 in the third octet → wildcard 3 there. Beware answers that hand you the subnet mask (contiguous 1s then 0s) instead of the wildcard (0s then 1s).

questions.stem: A router has these routes to 10.1.1.50: an OSPF route 10.1.1.0/24, a static route 10.1.1.0/25, and an EIGRP route 10.1.1.48/29. Which is used to forward the packet to 10.1.1.50?

options.text: The OSPF /24 route (lowest administrative distance among IGPs)

explanation.correct: The routing table chooses the LONGEST PREFIX MATCH first. 10.1.1.48/29 (covers .48–.55) is the most specific route containing .50, so it wins regardless of administrative distance.

distractors.A: AD only breaks ties between routes to the SAME prefix; it is not consulted when prefixes differ in length.
distractors.B: Static has the lowest AD, but AD is irrelevant here because the prefixes differ.
distractors.D: Load-balancing happens only across equal-cost routes to the same prefix.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order of operations: (1) longest prefix match, then (2) AD to break ties for identical prefixes, then (3) metric within the same protocol.

questions.stem: You want a backup default route via 203.0.113.2 that is used ONLY if the OSPF-learned default route (AD 110) disappears. Which command creates it?

explanation.correct: A floating static route needs an AD HIGHER than the protocol it backs up. OSPF is AD 110, so 120 keeps the static out of the table until the OSPF route is gone.

distractors.B: AD 90 is lower than OSPF's 110, so this static would WIN and be used all the time — not a backup.
distractors.C: No AD means the default AD of 1, which beats OSPF and is always active.
distractors.D: AD 1 (even with 'permanent') also beats OSPF and would be used immediately.

explanation.exam_pattern: Floating static = set AD ABOVE the primary source's AD. Know the defaults: connected 0, static 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120.

questions.stem: How does an OSPFv2 router choose its router-id if no 'router-id' command is configured and OSPF is started after interfaces are up?

options.text: Highest IP address on any active loopback; otherwise highest IP on any active interface
Lowest IP address on any active interface
The MAC address of the first interface

explanation.correct: RID selection order: (1) explicit 'router-id', (2) highest IP on an up loopback, (3) highest IP on any up physical interface. Loopbacks win because they are stable.

distractors.B: OSPF uses the HIGHEST interface IP, not the lowest.
distractors.C: OSPF RIDs are 32-bit values in dotted-decimal, derived from IPs, not MACs.
distractors.D: A RID is always chosen at process start if addresses exist; it is not left at 0.

explanation.exam_pattern: router-id > highest loopback > highest active interface. Changing it later needs 'clear ip ospf process' to take effect.

questions.stem: Two routers run HSRPv2 for gateway 10.0.0.1. R1 has priority 110 with preempt; R2 has priority 100. R1 reloads, R2 becomes active, then R1 comes back. What happens?

options.text: R1 becomes active again because preempt is configured
R2 stays active; R1 becomes standby because it lacks preempt
Both routers become active, causing a conflict
The virtual IP changes to R2's physical address

explanation.correct: Preempt lets a higher-priority router reclaim the active role when it returns. R1 (110, preempt) will take the active role back from R2 (100).

distractors.B: Without preempt R1 would stay standby — but R1 DOES have preempt here, so it reclaims active.
distractors.C: HSRP elects exactly one active router; there is no dual-active in normal operation.
distractors.D: The virtual IP and virtual MAC (0000.0c07.acXX) are owned by whichever router is active; they do not change to a physical address.

explanation.exam_pattern: Higher HSRP priority + preempt = reclaims active. No preempt = the incumbent keeps active even if a higher-priority router returns. HSRPv2 vMAC = 0000.0C9F.FXXX.

questions.stem: On a 1 Gbps interface with the default OSPF reference bandwidth (100 Mbps), what is the OSPF cost of the interface? Enter the number.

explanation.correct: OSPF cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth = 100 Mbps / 1000 Mbps = 0.1, rounded UP to a minimum of 1. So Gigabit, 10 Gig, etc. all show cost 1 by default — which is why you raise the reference bandwidth.
explanation.exam_pattern: Default reference = 10^8 (100 Mbps). FastEthernet=1, Gig=1, 10Gig=1 (all floor to 1) — the reason to set 'auto-cost reference-bandwidth' consistently network-wide.

questions.stem: Which TWO parameters MUST match for two OSPFv2 routers to form a neighbor adjacency on a link?

options.text: OSPF area ID on the link

explanation.correct: To become neighbors, routers must agree on hello/dead timers and be in the same area (also same subnet/mask, matching auth, matching stub flags, and compatible MTU to go FULL).

distractors.C: Process IDs are locally significant — they can differ freely.
distractors.D: Router IDs must be UNIQUE, not matching; duplicate RIDs break OSPF.
distractors.E: Bandwidth affects cost/metric, not whether an adjacency forms.

explanation.exam_pattern: Must-match for adjacency: area, hello/dead, subnet+mask, auth, stub flag, MTU (for FULL). Must DIFFER: router-id. Don't-care: process ID.

questions.stem: Which NAT type lets many inside hosts share a single public IP by multiplexing on Layer 4 port numbers?

explanation.correct: PAT (Port Address Translation), configured with the 'overload' keyword, maps many inside addresses to one outside address by tracking unique source ports — the basis of typical home/office Internet access.

distractors.A: Static NAT is a fixed one-to-one mapping, often for inbound servers.
distractors.B: Dynamic NAT assigns from a pool but is still one-to-one while a mapping lasts.
distractors.D: Twice NAT translates both source and destination; it is not the many-to-one sharing mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: Keyword 'overload' = PAT = many-to-one using ports. 'inside/outside' and 'local/global' terminology is the other favorite NAT trap.

questions.stem: Clients on a subnet with no local DHCP server receive no addresses. The server is on another subnet. Which command on the clients' gateway SVI fixes this?

explanation.correct: 'ip helper-address' turns the router/SVI into a DHCP relay: it converts the client broadcast DISCOVER into a unicast to the server across subnets (and relays other key UDP broadcasts).

distractors.B: excluded-address reserves addresses within a LOCAL pool; it does not relay to a remote server.
distractors.C: Creating a local pool would make this router the server, not relay to the existing one.
distractors.D: 'service dhcp' just enables the DHCP feature globally (on by default); it does not forward across subnets.

explanation.exam_pattern: Cross-subnet DHCP = relay via 'ip helper-address' on the interface facing the clients. Remember DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack.

verify_cli: show ip interface g0/0 | include Helper

questions.stem: An NTP server shows 'stratum 2'. What does the stratum value indicate?

options.text: The number of clients synchronized to it
Its distance (hop count) from an authoritative reference clock

explanation.correct: Stratum measures distance from the reference clock. Stratum 0 is the reference (atomic/GPS), stratum 1 is directly attached, stratum 2 syncs to a stratum-1 server, and so on. Lower stratum = more authoritative.

distractors.A: Stratum has nothing to do with how many clients use the server.
distractors.C: Polling interval is a separate NTP parameter, not the stratum.
distractors.D: NTP version (e.g., v3/v4) is unrelated to the stratum number.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lower stratum = closer to the true time source. A device syncing to a stratum-N server becomes stratum N+1.

questions.stem: A logging policy says to capture messages of severity 'warning' and more severe. Which 'logging trap' level and numeric value is correct?

explanation.correct: Syslog severities run 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug); LOWER is more severe. 'logging trap 4' captures level 4 (warning) and everything numerically below it (0–4), i.e., warning and more severe.

distractors.B: Level 7 (debugging) captures EVERYTHING 0–7, far more than warnings-and-above.
distractors.C: Level 2 (critical) would miss levels 3 (error) and 4 (warning).
distractors.D: Level 0 captures only emergencies.

explanation.exam_pattern: Mnemonic 0–7: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Icecream Daily (Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Info, Debug). Setting level N logs 0..N.

questions.stem: Security requires authentication AND encryption of SNMP management traffic. Which SNMP configuration meets both requirements?

options.text: SNMPv2c with a complex community string

explanation.correct: Only SNMPv3 offers encryption, and the 'priv' level provides BOTH authentication (authPriv) and privacy/encryption of the payload.

distractors.A: SNMPv2c sends community strings in clear text — no encryption at all.
distractors.B: 'auth' (authNoPriv) authenticates but does NOT encrypt the data.
distractors.D: SNMPv1 with an ACL limits who can connect but still sends data in clear text.

explanation.exam_pattern: SNMPv3 levels: noAuthNoPriv < authNoPriv < authPriv. Only 'priv' (authPriv) encrypts. v1/v2c never encrypt.

questions.stem: Which DSCP marking is the standard recommendation for latency-sensitive VoIP media (RTP) traffic placed in a priority queue?

explanation.correct: EF (DSCP 46) is the per-hop behavior reserved for low-latency, low-jitter traffic like voice media, typically serviced by a priority (LLQ) queue.

distractors.B: CS1 (8) is 'scavenger'-class, the LOWEST priority — the opposite of voice.
distractors.C: AF11 is a low-drop assured-forwarding class, used for some data, not voice media.
distractors.D: DSCP 0 is best-effort with no QoS guarantee, unsuitable for real-time voice.

explanation.exam_pattern: Voice media = EF (46), priority queue. Call signaling = CS3 (24). Scavenger = CS1 (8). Best effort = 0.

questions.stem: An extended ACL is applied to deny host 10.1.1.10 from reaching web server 203.0.113.5. Where should it be placed, per Cisco best practice?

options.text: Inbound, closest to the source (10.1.1.10's router interface)
Outbound, closest to the destination server
Inbound on every interface in the path
It does not matter where an extended ACL is placed

explanation.correct: Extended ACLs match source AND destination, so place them close to the SOURCE to drop unwanted traffic early and save bandwidth across the network.

distractors.B: That is the rule for STANDARD ACLs (match source only → place near destination to avoid over-blocking).
distractors.C: Applying it everywhere wastes resources and risks unintended drops.
distractors.D: Placement absolutely matters for efficiency and correctness.

explanation.exam_pattern: Extended → near SOURCE. Standard → near DESTINATION. Remember the implicit 'deny any' at the end of every ACL.

verify_cli: show ip interface g0/0 | include access list

questions.stem: A port-security violation occurs. The port should DROP offending frames and increment a counter but remain up (no err-disable). Which violation mode is this?

explanation.correct: 'restrict' drops violating frames, increments the violation counter, and sends an SNMP trap/syslog — while keeping the port up.

distractors.A: 'protect' also drops frames but does NOT increment the counter or alert.
distractors.C: 'shutdown' (the default) err-disables the port entirely on violation.
distractors.D: 'shutdown vlan' err-disables only the offending VLAN on the port, not the standard counting behaviour described.

explanation.exam_pattern: protect = silent drop; restrict = drop + count + alert; shutdown = err-disable (default). The counter + stays-up combo points to restrict.

questions.stem: After enabling DHCP snooping, clients connected through the uplink to the real DHCP server stop getting addresses. What is the MOST likely fix?

options.text: Configure the uplink toward the DHCP server as a trusted port
Configure the client access ports as trusted
Disable DHCP snooping on the server VLAN
Add 'ip dhcp snooping information option' on client ports

explanation.correct: DHCP snooping treats all ports as UNtrusted by default, dropping server-sourced messages (OFFER/ACK) on them. The port toward the legitimate DHCP server must be marked trusted with 'ip dhcp snooping trust'.

distractors.B: Access ports facing clients should stay UNtrusted — trusting them defeats the protection against rogue servers.
distractors.C: Disabling snooping removes the security entirely rather than fixing the trust boundary.
distractors.D: Option-82 insertion is unrelated to the server replies being dropped; and it often must be managed carefully across relays.

explanation.exam_pattern: Snooping default = untrusted everywhere. Trust only the ports toward real DHCP servers/uplinks. Client ports stay untrusted (rate-limited).

questions.stem: Which line correctly permits ONLY the single host 192.168.1.17 in a standard numbered ACL?

explanation.correct: 'host 192.168.1.17' is shorthand for the wildcard 0.0.0.0 (match exactly this address). It is the correct, idiomatic single-host match.

distractors.B: 255.255.255.255 as a wildcard means 'match ANY address' — the opposite of one host.
distractors.C: 0.0.0.255 matches the whole 192.168.1.0/24, not a single host.
distractors.D: 0.0.0.0 wildcard is right, but the base address is .0 (the network), not .17.

explanation.exam_pattern: host X == X 0.0.0.0. any == 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255. Watch for the classic swap of subnet mask vs wildcard.

questions.stem: In an 802.1X deployment, which device plays the role of the 'authenticator'?

options.text: The end-user PC running the 802.1X client
The access switch controlling port access

explanation.correct: The authenticator is the switch (or WLC): it sits between the supplicant and the authentication server, controlling the port and relaying EAP to RADIUS.

distractors.A: The PC/software is the SUPPLICANT.
distractors.C: The RADIUS server (e.g., ISE) is the AUTHENTICATION SERVER.
distractors.D: AD is an identity store the auth server queries, not an 802.1X role itself.

explanation.exam_pattern: Three roles: Supplicant (client) ↔ Authenticator (switch/WLC) ↔ Authentication Server (RADIUS). EAP between supplicant/authenticator; RADIUS between authenticator/server.

questions.stem: Which Layer 2 attack is directly mitigated by enabling BPDU Guard on access (PortFast) ports?

options.text: A rogue switch injecting superior BPDUs to become root

explanation.correct: BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast port the instant it receives ANY BPDU, stopping an unauthorized switch from participating in STP or hijacking the root role on an access port.

distractors.B: MAC flooding is mitigated by port security, not BPDU Guard.
distractors.C: DHCP starvation is handled by DHCP snooping + port security.
distractors.D: ARP poisoning is mitigated by Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI).

explanation.exam_pattern: Match the tool to the attack: BPDU Guard→rogue STP/BPDUs; Port security→MAC flooding; DHCP snooping→rogue DHCP/starvation; DAI→ARP spoofing.

questions.stem: Which pair of IPsec protocols/services provides BOTH confidentiality (encryption) and data integrity for a site-to-site VPN?

explanation.correct: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) provides encryption AND integrity/authentication of the payload. AH provides integrity/authentication but NO encryption.

distractors.B: AH authenticates but does not encrypt, so it fails the confidentiality requirement.
distractors.C: GRE is a tunneling protocol with no encryption by itself (often paired with IPsec).
distractors.D: HSRP is a first-hop redundancy protocol, unrelated to VPN security.

explanation.exam_pattern: ESP = encryption + integrity. AH = integrity only (no encryption). IKE/ISAKMP negotiates the keys. GRE adds multiprotocol tunneling, not security.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts NETCONF and RESTCONF?

options.text: NETCONF uses SSH (port 830) and XML; RESTCONF uses HTTPS and XML or JSON
NETCONF uses HTTP verbs on port 443; RESTCONF uses SNMP
Both use SNMPv3 as their transport
RESTCONF uses SSH port 22; NETCONF uses Telnet

explanation.correct: NETCONF runs over SSH (TCP 830) and encodes data in XML, with explicit datastores and RPCs. RESTCONF is a REST/HTTPS interface to the same YANG models and supports XML or JSON encoding.

distractors.B: NETCONF does not use HTTP verbs; RESTCONF (not NETCONF) is the HTTP/REST one, and neither uses SNMP.
distractors.C: Neither protocol uses SNMP as transport; both are model-driven (YANG) alternatives to SNMP.
distractors.D: RESTCONF uses HTTPS (443), not SSH/22; NETCONF uses SSH/830, not Telnet.

explanation.exam_pattern: NETCONF = SSH 830, XML, datastores (running/candidate/startup), RPCs. RESTCONF = HTTPS 443, XML/JSON, HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE). Both driven by YANG models.

questions.stem: A RESTCONF client sends an HTTP PUT and receives '201 Created'. What does this status code indicate?

options.text: The request was malformed and rejected
The server encountered an internal error

explanation.correct: 2xx codes indicate success; 201 specifically means a new resource was created as a result of the request.

distractors.A: A malformed request returns 4xx, typically 400 Bad Request.
distractors.C: Authentication failure returns 401 Unauthorized (or 403 Forbidden).
distractors.D: A server-side error returns 5xx, e.g., 500 Internal Server Error.

explanation.exam_pattern: HTTP ranges: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400/401/403/404), 5xx server error.

questions.stem: In the JSON below, what is the data type of the value associated with the key "interfaces"?

explanation.correct: Square brackets [ ] denote a JSON array (an ordered list). Here "interfaces" maps to a list of three strings.

distractors.A: Objects use curly braces { } with key:value pairs.
distractors.C: A string would be in double quotes with no brackets, e.g., "Gi0/0".
distractors.D: Booleans are the literals true/false (like "enabled" here), not a bracketed list.

explanation.exam_pattern: JSON types: {} object, [] array, "" string, numbers, true/false, null. Count brackets to identify the structure.

questions.stem: Which configuration-management tool is AGENTLESS and pushes configuration to devices over SSH using YAML 'playbooks'?

explanation.correct: Ansible is agentless (uses SSH/NETCONF), uses a push model, and defines automation in YAML playbooks — a good fit for network devices that can't run agents.

distractors.B: Puppet is agent-based (pull model) and uses its own declarative DSL (manifests), typically over TCP 8140.
distractors.C: Chef is agent-based (pull), uses Ruby-based 'recipes'/'cookbooks'.
distractors.D: SaltStack commonly uses minions (agents), though it has an agentless SSH mode.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ansible = agentless, push, YAML, SSH. Puppet/Chef = agent, pull (manifests/recipes). This push/pull + agent distinction is the usual question.

questions.stem: In an SDN controller-based architecture, which interface does the controller use to communicate DOWN to the network devices (the forwarding plane)?

explanation.correct: Southbound interfaces (e.g., NETCONF, OpenFlow, Cisco OnePK) connect the controller DOWN to the devices it programs. Northbound APIs face UP toward applications/orchestration.

distractors.A: Northbound faces UP to apps/scripts (often REST), not down to devices.
distractors.C: A management VLAN is not an SDN controller interface concept.
distractors.D: East-west is controller-to-controller communication, not controller-to-device.

explanation.exam_pattern: Northbound = up to apps (REST). Southbound = down to devices (NETCONF/OpenFlow). Think of the controller in the middle of the sandwich.

questions.stem: What is the primary benefit of using a controller-based network with 'intent-based' automation compared to traditional per-device CLI?

options.text: It removes the need for any IP addressing
Centralized, consistent policy with reduced configuration drift and human error
It eliminates the need for routing protocols entirely
It makes all links automatically faster

explanation.correct: Controller-based/intent-based automation translates business intent into consistent device configuration centrally, reducing drift, speeding changes, and minimizing manual per-box errors.

distractors.A: Devices still need IP addressing; automation does not remove it.
distractors.C: Underlay routing is still required (often automated), not eliminated.
distractors.D: Automation does not change physical link speeds.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automation benefits = consistency, speed, scalability, fewer errors, less drift. Watch for 'eliminates X entirely' distractors — automation manages, it doesn't abolish fundamentals.

questions.stem: A host is assigned 192.168.10.100/27. What is the first usable host address of that subnet?

explanation.correct: A /27 (255.255.255.224) has block size 32, so subnets are .0, .32, .64, .96, .128… The host .100 is in the .96 subnet (range .96–.127). The network is .96 and the first usable host is .97.

distractors.A: 192.168.10.96 is the network (subnet) address, not a usable host.
distractors.C: 192.168.10.65 belongs to the .64 subnet, one block too low.
distractors.D: 192.168.10.99 is usable but is not the FIRST usable address.

explanation.exam_pattern: Block size = 256 − mask octet. Find the subnet .100 lands in, then network+1 is the first host, broadcast−1 is the last host.

questions.stem: How many usable host addresses are available in a 255.255.255.248 subnet?

explanation.correct: 255.255.255.248 is /29, leaving 3 host bits: 2^3 − 2 = 6 usable hosts (subtract the network and broadcast addresses).

distractors.A: 8 is the total addresses in the block (2^3), before subtracting network+broadcast.
distractors.C: 4 would be a /30 (2^2 − 2 = 2)… even that isn't 4; this is just a trap value.
distractors.D: 14 usable corresponds to a /28 (2^4 − 2), not /29.

explanation.exam_pattern: Usable = 2^(host bits) − 2. /29 → 3 host bits → 6. Memorize the small masks: /30=2, /29=6, /28=14, /27=30.

questions.stem: A point-to-point WAN link needs exactly 2 usable host addresses and no waste. Enter the prefix length (e.g. 30) you should use.

explanation.correct: 2 host bits give 2^2 − 2 = 2 usable addresses — exactly enough for the two router interfaces on a point-to-point link. 32 − 2 = /30.
explanation.exam_pattern: Point-to-point links are the classic /30 case (or /31 with ip unnumbered-style addressing). Smallest subnet that yields 2 hosts.

questions.stem: Which subnet does the host 10.40.60.200/21 belong to?

explanation.correct: A /21 has 255.255.248.0, block size 8 in the 3rd octet: .0, .8, .16, … .48, .56, .64. The 3rd octet 60 falls in the .56 block (56–63), so the subnet is 10.40.56.0/21.

distractors.B: 10.40.60.0 is not a /21 boundary; /21 boundaries in the 3rd octet are multiples of 8 (56, 64), not 60.
distractors.C: 10.40.64.0 is the NEXT /21 subnet; 60 has not reached 64 yet.

explanation.exam_pattern: When the mask falls in the 3rd octet, block size = 256 − mask3. Round the 3rd octet DOWN to the nearest multiple of the block size.

questions.stem: A department needs at least 500 hosts in a single subnet carved from 172.20.0.0. Which mask uses the fewest host bits that still fit?

explanation.correct: 500 hosts needs 9 host bits (2^9 − 2 = 510 ≥ 500); 8 bits give only 254. 9 host bits = /23 = 255.255.254.0.

distractors.B: /24 gives 254 usable hosts — not enough for 500.
distractors.C: /22 (1022 usable) fits but wastes addresses; it does not use the FEWEST host bits.
distractors.D: /25 gives only 126 usable hosts.

explanation.exam_pattern: Find the smallest host-bit count where 2^n − 2 ≥ requirement, then prefix = 32 − n. 500 → 9 bits → /23.

questions.stem: Which IPv6 prefix identifies a link-local address?

explanation.correct: Link-local addresses come from FE80::/10 and are auto-configured on every IPv6 interface; they are used for neighbor discovery and next-hop addressing and are never routed off the link.

distractors.B: FC00::/7 is unique local (ULA), the IPv6 equivalent of RFC1918 private space.
distractors.C: 2000::/3 is global unicast (routable Internet addresses).
distractors.D: FF00::/8 is the multicast range.

explanation.exam_pattern: Memorize the ranges: FE80::/10 link-local, FC00::/7 ULA, 2000::/3 global unicast, FF00::/8 multicast, ::1 loopback.

questions.stem: What is the correctly compressed form of 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?

explanation.correct: Drop leading zeros in each hextet and replace the one longest all-zero run with a single ::. The six 0000 hextets collapse to ::, and 0001 → 1, giving 2001:DB8::1.

distractors.B: Leaves zero hextets explicit and only partially compresses — not the fully compressed form.
distractors.C: 0001 should drop its leading zeros to 1.
distractors.D: Three colons (:::) is invalid; :: is exactly two colons and appears once.

explanation.exam_pattern: One :: only, replacing the LONGEST zero run; drop leading zeros per hextet. Watch for ::: and for un-dropped leading zeros.

questions.stem: At which OSI layer does a traditional Layer 2 switch make its forwarding decision, and based on what address?

options.text: Layer 2, using the destination MAC address
Layer 3, using the destination IP address
Layer 1, using the physical port number
Layer 4, using the destination port number

explanation.correct: A Layer 2 switch forwards frames using the destination MAC address, looked up in its MAC address table. Unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast frames are flooded out all ports in the VLAN except the source.

distractors.B: Routing on destination IP is a Layer 3 function (router / L3 switch).
distractors.C: Layer 1 is bits on the wire; it makes no forwarding decision.
distractors.D: Layer 4 ports are used by firewalls/PAT, not basic switch forwarding.

explanation.exam_pattern: Switch = L2 = MAC table. Router = L3 = routing table/IP. Map the device to the layer and the address type together.

questions.stem: Which well-known port pair is used by a DHCP client and server?

explanation.correct: DHCP uses UDP: the server listens on port 67 and the client uses port 68. The DORA exchange (Discover, Offer, Request, Ack) runs over these UDP ports, which is why a DHCP relay (ip helper-address) is needed across subnets since broadcasts don't route.

distractors.B: DHCP is UDP, not TCP.
distractors.C: UDP 53 is DNS and UDP 123 is NTP.
distractors.D: UDP 69 is TFTP and UDP 161 is SNMP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Learn the port table cold: DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, TFTP 69, HTTP 80, NTP 123, SNMP 161/162, HTTPS 443, Syslog 514.

questions.stem: Which TWO are characteristics of TCP but NOT UDP?

options.text: A three-way handshake establishes the session
Lost segments are retransmitted using sequence/acknowledgment numbers
It adds the least possible header overhead for real-time voice
It is connectionless with no delivery guarantee
It uses a source and destination port number

explanation.correct: TCP is connection-oriented: it opens with a SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK three-way handshake and guarantees delivery by sequencing segments and retransmitting any that are not acknowledged.

distractors.C: Low overhead for real-time voice describes UDP, not TCP.
distractors.D: Connectionless with no guarantee describes UDP.
distractors.E: Both TCP and UDP use source/destination ports, so it does not distinguish them.

explanation.exam_pattern: TCP = handshake + reliability (seq/ack, retransmit, windowing). UDP = fast, connectionless, best-effort. Shared traits (ports) are traps.

questions.stem: A switch receives a unicast frame whose destination MAC is not in its MAC address table. What does the switch do?

options.text: Floods the frame out all ports in the VLAN except the one it arrived on
Drops the frame and sends an ICMP unreachable
Forwards it only to the default gateway
Buffers the frame until the destination replies to an ARP

explanation.correct: An unknown unicast is flooded out every port in the same VLAN except the ingress port. When the destination replies, the switch learns its MAC and future frames are forwarded only out that port.

distractors.B: Switches don't generate ICMP unreachables; that's a Layer 3 behavior.
distractors.C: A switch has no concept of a default gateway for frame forwarding.
distractors.D: The switch floods immediately; it doesn't buffer waiting on ARP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unknown unicast, broadcast, and multicast are flooded within the VLAN. Known unicast is forwarded out a single port.

questions.stem: On a LAN switch, how many collision domains and broadcast domains exist if all 24 access ports are in the same VLAN?

explanation.correct: Each switch port is its own collision domain (full-duplex micro-segmentation), so 24 ports = 24 collision domains. A VLAN is one broadcast domain, and all ports share one VLAN here, so 1 broadcast domain.

distractors.B: Reversed: ports are separate collision domains; the single VLAN is one broadcast domain.
distractors.C: Ports in the same VLAN share one broadcast domain, not 24.
distractors.D: A hub would be one collision domain; a switch separates them per port.

explanation.exam_pattern: Collision domain = per switch port. Broadcast domain = per VLAN. Routers/subinterfaces and VLANs bound broadcast domains.

questions.stem: Which cable type is appropriate to connect a PC NIC directly to a router interface when Auto-MDIX is disabled on both?

options.text: Crossover (T568A on one end, T568B on the other)

explanation.correct: A PC and a router are both 'like' (end-host/router) devices that transmit on the same pins, so without Auto-MDIX they need a crossover cable to swap transmit and receive pairs.

distractors.B: Straight-through is for unlike devices (PC↔switch, router↔switch).
distractors.C: A rollover cable is for console/management access, not data.
distractors.D: Fiber would require fiber interfaces on both ends; copper crossover is the answer for RJ-45 NIC-to-router.

explanation.exam_pattern: Like-to-like (PC↔router, switch↔switch, PC↔PC) = crossover. Unlike (PC↔switch, router↔switch) = straight-through. Auto-MDIX hides this but the exam may disable it.

questions.stem: In the 2.4 GHz band, which THREE channels are commonly used because they do not overlap in North America?

explanation.correct: 2.4 GHz channels are 22 MHz wide but spaced only 5 MHz apart, so most overlap. Channels 1, 6, and 11 are far enough apart (25 MHz centers) to be non-overlapping, which is why they're used for cell planning.

distractors.D: Channel 3 overlaps both 1 and 6.

explanation.exam_pattern: 2.4 GHz → 1/6/11 are the non-overlapping trio. 5 GHz has many more non-overlapping channels, which is a common comparison.

questions.stem: Which 802.11 amendment operates in BOTH the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands and introduces OFDMA to improve efficiency in dense client environments?

explanation.correct: 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) works in both 2.4 and 5 GHz and adds OFDMA, which lets an AP serve many clients in parallel within a channel — a big gain in high-density deployments.

distractors.B: 802.11ac operates only in 5 GHz and does not use OFDMA.
distractors.C: 802.11n (2.4/5 GHz) introduced MIMO but not OFDMA.
distractors.D: 802.11g is 2.4 GHz only, up to 54 Mbps, no OFDMA.

explanation.exam_pattern: ax = Wi-Fi 6 = both bands + OFDMA. ac = Wi-Fi 5 = 5 GHz only. n = first dual-band with MIMO. Match amendment → band → key feature.

questions.stem: On an 802.1Q trunk, how is traffic for the native VLAN transmitted?

explanation.correct: 802.1Q leaves the native VLAN untagged on a trunk — frames are sent without a dot1q tag. Both trunk ends must agree on the native VLAN or you get a CDP native-VLAN-mismatch and traffic leaks between VLANs.

distractors.B: The native VLAN (default VLAN 1, but configurable) is specifically the one that is NOT tagged.
distractors.C: 4094 is just a VLAN ID; tagging it is unrelated to native behavior.
distractors.D: Double-tagging is a QinQ/attack scenario, not normal native-VLAN handling.

explanation.exam_pattern: Native VLAN = untagged on the trunk; mismatched native VLANs trigger a %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH and are a security concern.

questions.stem: A port is configured with 'switchport mode dynamic auto' on both ends of a switch-to-switch link. What will the link become?

explanation.correct: DTP 'dynamic auto' will trunk only if the other side actively asks (trunk or dynamic desirable). Auto-to-auto means neither side initiates, so the link stays an access port in the access VLAN.

distractors.B: A trunk needs at least one side to be 'trunk' or 'dynamic desirable'.
distractors.C: Modern Catalyst switches use 802.1Q, not ISL, and no trunk forms here anyway.
distractors.D: EtherChannel is unrelated to DTP negotiation.

explanation.exam_pattern: DTP matrix: auto+auto = access; desirable or trunk on one side = trunk; access on one side = access. Best practice: hardcode mode.

questions.stem:
Four switches run PVST+ for VLAN 10. Their bridge priorities and MACs are:
SW1 32778 / 0012.0012.0012
SW2 32778 / 0011.0011.0011
SW3 28682 / 0013.0013.0013
SW4 32778 / 0010.0010.0010
Which switch becomes the root bridge for VLAN 10?

explanation.correct: The root is the lowest bridge ID = priority (incl. the VLAN sys-id-ext) then MAC as tiebreaker. SW3's 28682 is the lowest priority (28672 + 10), so SW3 wins outright regardless of MAC.

distractors.B: SW4 has the lowest MAC but its priority (32778) is higher than SW3's, and priority is compared first.
distractors.C: SW2 also has priority 32778; MAC is only a tiebreaker among equal priorities.
distractors.D: SW1 has the highest MAC among the 32778 group and a higher priority than SW3.

explanation.exam_pattern: Compare PRIORITY first (lower wins), MAC only breaks ties. PVST+ priority = base + VLAN sys-id-ext, so 28672+10 = 28682.

questions.stem: Using classic (short) STP path costs, what is the cost of a 1 Gbps link?

explanation.correct: Classic STP short-mode costs: 10 Mbps = 100, 100 Mbps = 19, 1 Gbps = 4, 10 Gbps = 2. A GigabitEthernet link therefore has a path cost of 4.

distractors.B: 19 is the cost of a 100 Mbps (FastEthernet) link.
distractors.C: 2 is the cost of a 10 Gbps link.
distractors.D: 100 is the cost of a 10 Mbps Ethernet link.

explanation.exam_pattern: Memorize the short-cost table: 10M=100, 100M=19, 1G=4, 10G=2. Root path cost is the sum of costs toward the root bridge.

questions.stem: Which interface-level feature immediately transitions an access port to the forwarding state for end devices, skipping listening/learning?

explanation.correct: PortFast lets an access port carrying a single host go straight to forwarding, avoiding the ~30 s listening/learning delay. It should only be on edge ports, and is normally paired with BPDU Guard for safety.

distractors.B: BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast port if it receives a BPDU; it doesn't speed up transition.
distractors.C: Root Guard prevents a port from becoming a root port (stops a rogue root).
distractors.D: UplinkFast speeds up root-port failover on wiring-closet switches, not edge port transition.

explanation.exam_pattern: PortFast = fast edge-port forwarding. Pair with BPDU Guard. Don't confuse with the Guards (BPDU/Root/Loop), which protect topology.

questions.stem: SW1 Gi0/1-2 is set to 'channel-group 1 mode active'. Which setting on SW2's matching ports will successfully form a LACP EtherChannel?

explanation.correct: LACP uses active/passive. Active↔active and active↔passive both form a channel (at least one side must be active). Passive↔passive does not, because neither initiates.

distractors.B: 'desirable' is PAgP (Cisco), which cannot negotiate with LACP 'active'.
distractors.C: 'auto' is PAgP as well, incompatible with LACP.
distractors.D: 'on' forms a static channel with no negotiation; mixing 'on' with 'active' does NOT form a channel.

explanation.exam_pattern: LACP = active/passive; PAgP = desirable/auto. You can't mix protocols, you can't mix 'on' with a negotiating mode, and passive+passive / auto+auto never bundle.

questions.stem: An EtherChannel fails to come up. 'show etherchannel summary' shows the port flags as (I). What does that indicate?

options.text: The port is stand-alone / independent — it has not bundled
The port is in use and bundled successfully
The port is a Layer 3 routed member

explanation.correct: In 'show etherchannel summary', (I) means stand-alone/independent — the port did not bundle, usually because of mismatched speed/duplex, VLAN, allowed-VLAN list, or EtherChannel mode between the two sides.

distractors.B: A bundled, in-use port shows the (P) flag, not (I).
distractors.C: Administratively down would show (D).
distractors.D: Layer 3 membership is unrelated to the (I) flag.

explanation.exam_pattern: Flag legend: (P)=bundled, (I)=stand-alone, (D)=down, (s)=suspended. (I)/(s) point at a config mismatch across the member ports.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about CDP and LLDP are correct?

options.text: CDP is Cisco-proprietary; LLDP (802.1AB) is an open standard
LLDP is enabled by default on Cisco switches, CDP is not
Both discover directly connected neighbors at Layer 2
CDP requires IP addresses on the link to exchange neighbor info
LLDP cannot report a neighbor's platform or port ID

explanation.correct: CDP is Cisco-proprietary while LLDP is the IEEE 802.1AB open standard, and both are Layer 2 discovery protocols that learn directly connected neighbors without needing Layer 3 reachability.

distractors.B: Reversed: CDP is on by default on Cisco gear; LLDP must be enabled.
distractors.D: CDP works at Layer 2 and needs no IP addressing on the link.
distractors.E: LLDP does report system name, platform, and port ID via its TLVs.

explanation.exam_pattern: CDP = Cisco, on by default; LLDP = open (802.1AB), off by default. Both are L2 and need no IP. Great for mapping topology.

questions.stem: In a split-MAC (lightweight) wireless architecture, which protocol carries control and data traffic between a lightweight AP and the WLC?

explanation.correct: Lightweight APs tunnel to the WLC using CAPWAP (Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points): a control channel on UDP 5246 and a data channel on UDP 5247. The WLC handles the heavy MAC functions (auth, mobility, RF), hence 'split-MAC'.

distractors.B: LWAPP is the older Cisco predecessor; modern deployments use CAPWAP.
distractors.C: CAPWAP (which uses DTLS for the control channel) is the standard, not raw GRE.
distractors.D: 802.1Q is wired VLAN tagging, not the AP-to-WLC tunnel.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lightweight AP ↔ WLC = CAPWAP (UDP 5246 control / 5247 data), split-MAC. Autonomous APs have no controller.

questions.stem: Which lightweight AP mode allows an AP at a branch to keep switching client traffic locally if the CAPWAP tunnel to a central WLC goes down?

explanation.correct: FlexConnect (formerly H-REAP) lets a branch AP switch client data locally onto the branch VLANs and keep authenticating clients even if the WAN link/CAPWAP tunnel to a central WLC fails.

distractors.B: In Local mode all client traffic is tunneled back to the WLC; a tunnel loss drops service.
distractors.C: Monitor mode APs don't serve clients; they scan for IDS/location.
distractors.D: Sniffer mode captures wireless frames for analysis, not client service.

explanation.exam_pattern: FlexConnect = branch survivability + local switching. Local = centralized tunneling. Monitor/Sniffer/Rogue-detector don't serve clients.

questions.stem: On a Cisco WLC, which interface type is mapped to a WLAN (SSID) to place its wireless clients into a specific VLAN/subnet?

explanation.correct: A dynamic interface on the WLC is tied to a client VLAN; mapping a WLAN to that dynamic interface puts the SSID's clients into that VLAN/subnet (and its DHCP scope).

distractors.B: The management interface is for controller management/CAPWAP discovery, not general client placement.
distractors.C: The service port is an out-of-band management port.
distractors.D: The virtual interface (e.g. 192.0.2.1) is used for web auth, DHCP relay, and mobility — not client VLAN mapping.

explanation.exam_pattern: WLC interfaces: management (control), virtual (web-auth/DHCP relay), service-port (OOB), dynamic (client VLANs). WLAN→dynamic interface sets the client subnet.

questions.stem: A trunk should carry only VLANs 10, 20 and 30. Enter the interface command that restricts the trunk to exactly those VLANs (use 'Gi' style, no abbreviation of keywords).

explanation.correct: 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30' replaces the allowed list with exactly those VLANs. Use 'add'/'remove' to edit an existing list without overwriting it.
explanation.exam_pattern: allowed vlan <list> = set exactly; allowed vlan add/remove = edit. Forgetting 'add' and overwriting the list is a classic outage cause.

questions.stem: A router has these routes to 10.1.1.0: a static 10.1.1.0/24, an OSPF 10.1.1.0/26, and an EIGRP 10.1.1.0/28. A packet is destined to 10.1.1.5. Which route is used to forward it?

options.text: The route with the lowest administrative distance

explanation.correct: Forwarding uses the LONGEST PREFIX MATCH first. 10.1.1.5 matches all three, but /28 is the most specific, so the EIGRP route wins — regardless of administrative distance.

distractors.B: /24 is the least specific match; longest prefix is checked before AD.
distractors.C: /26 is more specific than /24 but less specific than the /28.
distractors.D: AD only breaks ties between routes to the SAME prefix; here prefixes differ.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order: longest prefix match → (if same prefix from different sources) lowest AD → (same source) lowest metric.

questions.stem: Two routes to 192.168.5.0/24 are learned: one via OSPF and one via external EIGRP. Which is installed in the routing table, and why?

options.text: External EIGRP, because AD 170 < OSPF AD 110 is false — OSPF wins at 110
OSPF, because its administrative distance (110) is lower than external EIGRP (170)
External EIGRP, because EIGRP always beats OSPF
Both are installed for load balancing

explanation.correct: Same prefix from two sources → lowest administrative distance wins. OSPF is 110; external EIGRP is 170. 110 < 170, so the OSPF route is installed.

distractors.A: The conclusion is right (OSPF wins) but the reasoning is garbled; state it cleanly: 110 < 170.
distractors.C: Internal EIGRP (90) beats OSPF, but EXTERNAL EIGRP is 170, which loses to OSPF.
distractors.D: Different protocols don't load-balance together; only equal-cost routes from the same protocol do.

explanation.exam_pattern: AD table: Connected 0, Static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120, External EIGRP 170, iBGP 200. Lower wins for identical prefixes.

questions.stem: Which command creates a default route that sends all unknown traffic to next hop 203.0.113.1?

explanation.correct: A default route is 0.0.0.0 with a 0.0.0.0 mask (match anything), pointing to the next hop: 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1'. It becomes the gateway of last resort.

distractors.B: 255.255.255.255 is a /32 host mask, not the all-zeros default mask.
distractors.C: 'ip default-network' is a legacy classful mechanism, not the standard default-route command.
distractors.D: The network and mask are in the wrong positions; the destination/mask come first, then the next hop.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default route = ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop|exit-int>. It shows as S* and the gateway of last resort in 'show ip route'.

questions.stem: You want a backup static route via 10.0.0.2 that is used ONLY if the primary OSPF route to the same prefix fails. Which command configures the floating static route?

explanation.correct: A floating static needs an administrative distance HIGHER than the primary route's so it stays out of the table until the primary is gone. OSPF is AD 110, so a static AD of 130 (> 110) floats behind OSPF and installs only on failure.

distractors.B: AD 90 is lower than OSPF's 110, so this static would WIN and be used all the time — not a backup.
distractors.C: The default static AD is 1, which always beats OSPF; again not a backup.
distractors.D: 'permanent' keeps the route even if the next hop is unreachable; it does not set a higher AD for failover.

explanation.exam_pattern: Floating static = static route with AD set ABOVE the primary protocol's AD so it only installs when the primary disappears.

questions.stem: Two OSPF routers are stuck in the EXSTART/EXCHANGE state and never reach FULL. Which mismatch most commonly causes this specific symptom?

options.text: An MTU mismatch on the connecting interfaces
Different OSPF process IDs on the two routers

explanation.correct: Routers get stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE when interface MTUs differ: OSPF checks MTU in DBD packets and refuses to progress if they don't match. Fix the MTU (or use 'ip ospf mtu-ignore').

distractors.B: Mismatched hello/dead timers prevent the neighbor relationship from forming at all (stuck in INIT/never seen), not EXSTART.
distractors.C: Mismatched areas stop neighbors forming (no adjacency), they don't reach EXSTART.
distractors.D: Process IDs are locally significant and need not match for an adjacency.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE = MTU mismatch. Never forming at all = hello/dead, area, subnet, or auth mismatch.

questions.stem: On an OSPF broadcast (multi-access) segment, how is the Designated Router elected?

options.text: Highest OSPF interface priority; the router-ID breaks a tie
Highest IP address on the segment, always
The router that booted first, regardless of priority

explanation.correct: DR/BDR election compares OSPF interface priority (default 1, higher wins); if priorities tie, the highest router-ID wins. A priority of 0 makes a router ineligible to ever be DR/BDR.

distractors.B: Higher priority wins, not lower; and priority 0 opts out entirely.
distractors.C: The router-ID (often the highest loopback) is only the tiebreaker, not the primary criterion.
distractors.D: OSPF elections are non-preemptive, but the winner is still chosen by priority/RID, not boot order alone.

explanation.exam_pattern: DR election: priority (high wins, 0 = never) → router-ID (high wins). Non-preemptive, so an existing DR stays until it drops.

questions.stem: With the default OSPF reference bandwidth (100 Mbps), what is the OSPF cost of a GigabitEthernet (1000 Mbps) interface?

explanation.correct: OSPF cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth = 100 Mbps / 1000 Mbps = 0.1, which rounds UP to the minimum cost of 1. This is why Gig, 10-Gig, etc. all show cost 1 by default — and why you raise the reference bandwidth ('auto-cost reference-bandwidth') in fast networks.

distractors.B: Cost 10 would be a 10 Mbps link (100/10) — not Gigabit.
distractors.C: Cost 100 would correspond to a ~1 Mbps link.
distractors.D: Cost is never 0; it rounds up to a minimum of 1.

explanation.exam_pattern: cost = ref-BW / int-BW, minimum 1. Default ref-BW = 100 Mbps makes FastEthernet=1 and everything faster also =1, hiding differences.

questions.stem: How does a Cisco router choose its OSPF router-ID if no 'router-id' is configured under the process?

options.text: Highest IP among up loopback interfaces; else highest IP among up physical interfaces
Lowest IP address on any interface
The MAC address of the first interface

explanation.correct: Router-ID selection order: (1) the 'router-id' command if set; (2) the highest IP on an up/up loopback; (3) the highest IP on an up/up physical interface. Loopbacks are preferred because they stay up.

distractors.B: OSPF picks the HIGHEST IP, not the lowest.
distractors.C: OSPF RID is an IP-formatted value derived from interfaces, not a MAC.
distractors.D: Any loopback (or physical) can source the RID, not just a management port.

explanation.exam_pattern: RID order: configured → highest loopback → highest physical. Changing it needs 'clear ip ospf process' to take effect.

questions.stem: Enter the OSPF router configuration command that advertises interface 10.1.1.1/30 into area 0 by matching that exact /30 (use a wildcard mask).

explanation.correct: A /30 is mask 255.255.255.252, whose inverse (wildcard) is 0.0.0.3. The network statement uses the subnet address and the wildcard: 'network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0'.
explanation.exam_pattern: OSPF network statements use WILDCARD masks (inverse of the subnet mask). /30 → 0.0.0.3, /24 → 0.0.0.255, /26 → 0.0.0.63.

questions.stem: Which wildcard mask matches exactly the subnet 192.168.8.0/22?

distractors.B: 0.0.0.255 is the wildcard for a /24, not a /22.
distractors.C: 0.0.7.255 is the wildcard for a /21.
distractors.D: 0.0.255.255 is the wildcard for a /16.

explanation.exam_pattern: Wildcard = 255.255.255.255 − subnet mask (per octet). /22 → 0.0.3.255. Remember block sizes: 3 in the 3rd octet = 4 subnets of /22.

questions.stem: In HSRP version 1, group 10, what is the virtual MAC address used by the active router for the group's virtual IP?

explanation.correct: HSRPv1 virtual MAC = 0000.0C07.ACxx, where xx is the group number in HEX. Group 10 decimal = 0x0A, so the MAC is 0000.0C07.AC0A.

distractors.B: AC10 would be group 16 (0x10), not group 10 — the group is expressed in hex.
distractors.C: 0000.5E00.01xx is the VRRP virtual MAC format, not HSRP.
distractors.D: 0007.B4xx is the GLBP virtual MAC format.

explanation.exam_pattern: HSRPv1 vMAC 0000.0C07.ACxx (xx = group in hex). VRRP = 0000.5E00.01xx. GLBP = 0007.B400.xxyy. Convert the group to hex.

questions.stem: Two routers run HSRP for a gateway. R1 has priority 150 with preempt configured; R2 has the default priority. Which router is active, and what does preempt change?

options.text: R1 is active; preempt lets R1 reclaim active after it recovers from a failure
R2 is active because it has the lower priority
R1 is active, but without preempt R2 can never be standby

explanation.correct: Higher HSRP priority wins the active role (R1 at 150 > R2's default 100). Preempt matters on recovery: without it, a recovered higher-priority router would stay standby; with preempt, R1 takes active back.

distractors.B: Higher priority wins, not lower.
distractors.C: R2 still becomes standby regardless of preempt; preempt governs reclaiming active, not standby eligibility.
distractors.D: Plain HSRP is active/standby, not load-balancing (GLBP load-balances).

explanation.exam_pattern: HSRP: highest priority active (default 100), tie → highest IP. 'preempt' is required for a recovered primary to take active back.

questions.stem: A Layer 2-only switch (no IP routing) needs to reach a TFTP server in a different subnet for management. Which command gives the switch its default gateway?

explanation.correct: When a switch is not routing (ip routing disabled), its own management traffic uses 'ip default-gateway <addr>'. The SVI/management interface sends off-subnet packets to that gateway.

distractors.B: 'ip route 0.0.0.0 ...' only works when 'ip routing' is ENABLED (L3 switch/router); a pure L2 switch ignores it for its own traffic.
distractors.C: 'ip default-network' is a legacy routing command, not for L2 switch management.
distractors.D: Wrong syntax; the keyword is 'ip default-gateway'.

explanation.exam_pattern: L2 switch mgmt (no ip routing) → ip default-gateway. L3 device (ip routing on) → ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0.

questions.stem: Which command makes an OSPF interface advertise its subnet into OSPF but stop sending hellos out of it (so no adjacency forms there)?

explanation.correct: 'passive-interface' keeps the network advertised in OSPF but stops hello packets on that interface, so no neighbor adjacency forms — ideal for LAN/edge interfaces facing hosts.

distractors.B: Shutting the interface removes it entirely — the subnet is no longer advertised either.
distractors.C: Changing the network type still sends hellos; it just alters DR/BDR behavior.
distractors.D: Removing the network statement stops advertising the subnet AND adjacency.

explanation.exam_pattern: passive-interface = advertise the subnet, suppress hellos. Common on user-facing LAN ports to prevent rogue adjacencies.

questions.stem: In 'show ip route', what does an 'O*E2' code on a route indicate?

options.text: An OSPF external type-2 route that is also the default route candidate
A static route to a null interface

explanation.correct: 'O' = OSPF, 'E2' = external type 2 (redistributed; metric does not increase as it propagates), and the '*' marks it as a candidate default route (gateway of last resort).

distractors.B: Connected routes use the code 'C'.
distractors.C: Static routes use 'S' (and 'S*' for a default static).
distractors.D: Internal EIGRP uses 'D'; external EIGRP uses 'D EX'.

explanation.exam_pattern: Route codes: C connected, S static, O OSPF, D EIGRP, * default candidate. E1 adds internal cost along the path; E2 keeps a fixed external metric.

references: CCNA 200-301 Topic 3.1 interpreting the routing table

questions.stem: Which NAT type lets many inside hosts share ONE public IP by tracking unique Layer 4 port numbers?

explanation.correct: PAT (Port Address Translation / NAT overload) maps many inside addresses to one outside address by assigning each flow a unique source port, so thousands of hosts can share a single public IP.

distractors.B: Static NAT is a fixed one-to-one mapping — no sharing.
distractors.C: Dynamic NAT without 'overload' uses a pool one-to-one and exhausts when the pool runs out.
distractors.D: Twice NAT translates both source and destination; it isn't the many-to-one sharing mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: Share one public IP for many hosts = PAT/overload (keyword 'overload'). Static = 1:1 fixed. Dynamic pool = 1:1 temporary.

questions.stem: Enter the one global command that enables PAT, translating hosts matched by ACL 1 out of the interface using 'overload' on GigabitEthernet0/0.
correct: ip nat inside source list 1 interface gigabitethernet0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 interface gi0/0 overload

explanation.correct: PAT to an interface address: 'ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload'. ACL 1 selects the inside hosts; 'overload' enables port multiplexing onto the interface IP.
explanation.exam_pattern: Interface PAT = ip nat inside source list <acl> interface <out-int> overload. Don't forget to mark interfaces 'ip nat inside/outside'.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the DHCP client/server message exchange?

explanation.correct: DORA: the client broadcasts a DISCOVER, the server sends an OFFER, the client broadcasts a REQUEST for the offered address, and the server confirms with an ACK.

distractors.B: Discover must come first — the client has no address yet.
distractors.C: Discover is the first step, not Offer.
distractors.D: Offer precedes Request; the client requests what was offered.

explanation.exam_pattern: DORA = Discover → Offer → Request → Ack. Discover and Request are broadcast; a relay (ip helper-address) forwards them across subnets.

questions.stem: Clients on VLAN 20 get no DHCP address; the DHCP server is on a different subnet reachable through the router. Which configuration fixes this?

options.text: ip helper-address <server> on the VLAN 20 SVI
ip dhcp excluded-address on the server
switchport mode access on the SVI

explanation.correct: DHCP Discover/Request are broadcasts that routers don't forward. 'ip helper-address <server>' on the clients' gateway (the VLAN 20 SVI) turns those broadcasts into unicasts to the DHCP server, so clients across the router get addresses.

distractors.B: Excluded-address just reserves addresses from a pool; it doesn't relay requests across subnets.
distractors.C: PortFast speeds edge-port forwarding; it has nothing to do with DHCP relay.
distractors.D: An SVI isn't an access port; this command doesn't apply/help here.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP across subnets = ip helper-address on the clients' gateway interface (the relay). Broadcast won't route by itself.

questions.stem: Which DNS resource record maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?

explanation.correct: An AAAA ('quad-A') record maps a name to a 128-bit IPv6 address, the IPv6 counterpart of the A record.

distractors.B: An A record maps a name to a 32-bit IPv4 address.
distractors.C: A PTR record does reverse lookups (IP → name).
distractors.D: An MX record points to a mail exchanger for a domain.

explanation.exam_pattern: A = IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, CNAME = alias, PTR = reverse, MX = mail. 'ip name-server' and 'ip domain-lookup' enable resolution on IOS.

questions.stem: A technician types 'ping server1' on a router and it tries to resolve 'server1' as a host but hangs. Which command disables that name-lookup attempt so typos return to the prompt quickly?

explanation.correct: 'no ip domain-lookup' disables DNS resolution on the device, so a mistyped command isn't treated as a hostname and sent to a (often nonexistent) name server, avoiding the long resolve/timeout hang.

distractors.B: Removing a name-server address doesn't stop the device from attempting resolution (and broadcasting lookups).
distractors.C: 'service dns' is not the IOS command controlling client lookups.
distractors.D: 'ip dns server' turns the device into a DNS server; it's unrelated to disabling client lookups.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lab hang on a typo = DNS lookup. Fix: 'no ip domain-lookup'. This is a classic console quality-of-life command.

questions.stem: In NTP, what does a lower stratum number indicate?

options.text: A clock source closer to the authoritative reference (more accurate)
A less accurate, more distant time source
The number of hops to the default gateway

explanation.correct: NTP stratum counts distance from the authoritative reference clock. Stratum 1 is directly attached to a reference (e.g., GPS/atomic); each hop away increments the stratum, so lower = closer/more accurate (stratum 16 = unsynchronized).

distractors.B: That describes a HIGHER stratum number.
distractors.C: Stratum is unrelated to routing administrative distance.
distractors.D: Stratum measures clock-source distance, not gateway hops.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lower stratum = better. Stratum 1 = reference-attached; 16 = unsynced. 'ntp server' points a client; 'ntp master <n>' sets a local authoritative stratum.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an SNMP trap from an SNMP inform?

options.text: An inform is acknowledged by the manager; a trap is not
A trap is acknowledged; an inform is fire-and-forget
Traps use TCP; informs use UDP
Informs are only available in SNMPv1

explanation.correct: An SNMP inform request is acknowledged by the NMS (and retransmitted if no ack arrives), making it more reliable than a trap, which the agent sends without any acknowledgment.

distractors.B: Reversed — the inform is the acknowledged one.
distractors.C: Both typically use UDP (notifications to port 162); the difference is the acknowledgment, not the transport.
distractors.D: Informs were introduced with SNMPv2c, not v1.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inform = acknowledged/reliable; Trap = unacknowledged. SNMP polls on 161, notifications on 162. v3 adds auth/priv security.

questions.stem: A syslog message is logged at severity level 2. What severity is that?

explanation.correct: Syslog severities (0–7): 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging. Level 2 = Critical.

distractors.B: Error is level 3.
distractors.C: Warning is level 4.
distractors.D: Emergency is level 0.

explanation.exam_pattern: Mnemonic for 0–7: 'Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream, Daily' (Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notification, Informational, Debugging). Lower = more severe.

questions.stem: Which QoS mechanism BUFFERS excess traffic to smooth the rate (introducing delay) rather than dropping it?

explanation.correct: Shaping buffers traffic that exceeds a rate and releases it later, smoothing bursts at the cost of delay/jitter. It's typically applied outbound.

distractors.B: Policing enforces a rate by dropping (or re-marking) excess rather than buffering it.
distractors.C: Marking sets a QoS value (DSCP/CoS); it doesn't manage rate.
distractors.D: Classification identifies traffic; it doesn't act on the rate.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shaping = buffer/delay (smooth, outbound). Policing = drop/re-mark (hard limit, in or out). EF/DSCP 46 is the expedited (voice) class.

questions.stem: Which DSCP value is the standard marking for real-time voice (RTP) traffic?

explanation.correct: Expedited Forwarding (EF, DSCP 46) is the standard per-hop behavior for latency-sensitive voice media; it is usually serviced by a low-latency (priority) queue.

distractors.B: AF11 (10) is a low-priority assured-forwarding class, not voice.
distractors.C: CS0/DSCP 0 is default/best-effort.
distractors.D: AF41 (34) is commonly used for interactive VIDEO, not voice media.

explanation.exam_pattern: Voice = EF (46), priority queue. Signaling often CS3 (24). Video often AF41 (34). Best-effort = DSCP 0.

questions.stem: Best practice says a STANDARD ACL should be placed where, relative to the traffic it filters?

options.text: As close to the destination as possible
As close to the source as possible
On the router with the highest IP

explanation.correct: A standard ACL matches only the SOURCE address, so placing it near the source could unintentionally block that source from reaching OTHER destinations. Put it near the destination to filter only the intended flow.

distractors.B: Near-the-source is the rule for EXTENDED ACLs (which match source AND destination/port), so they can drop traffic early without over-blocking.
distractors.C: Placement is about traffic flow, not which router has the highest IP.
distractors.D: ACLs go on the interface/direction that filters the flow, not only the core.

explanation.exam_pattern: Standard ACL → near destination (source-only match). Extended ACL → near source (precise match, drop early).

questions.stem:
Consider this named ACL applied inbound on Gi0/0:
  permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 80
