  deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any
  permit ip any any
A host 10.1.1.5 sends an HTTPS (TCP 443) request. What happens?

options.text: It is denied by the second line (deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any)
It is permitted by the first line
It is permitted by the third line (permit ip any any)
It is denied by the implicit deny at the end

explanation.correct: ACLs are processed top-down, first match wins. HTTPS is TCP 443, so it does NOT match line 1 (port 80). It DOES match line 2 (deny ip from 10.1.1.0/24), so it is dropped there and later permit lines are never evaluated.

distractors.B: Line 1 only permits destination port 80; 443 doesn't match it.
distractors.C: Processing stops at the first match (line 2 deny); line 3 is never reached.
distractors.D: An explicit deny (line 2) is hit before the implicit deny would apply.

explanation.exam_pattern: Top-down, first-match, then stop. Order matters: a broad deny above a permit shadows it. Trace the specific packet against each line.

questions.stem: Enter the single ACE that permits only the host 192.168.1.50 (a standard numbered ACL line, using the 'host' keyword) — just the permit statement.

explanation.correct: A single host is matched with 'host 192.168.1.50' (equivalent to the wildcard 0.0.0.0): e.g. 'access-list 1 permit host 192.168.1.50'.
explanation.exam_pattern: host X == X 0.0.0.0 (match one address). 'any' == 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 (match all).

questions.stem: A port-security port is configured with the default violation mode. A second MAC appears and the port goes to err-disabled, sending a syslog/SNMP notification. Which violation mode is in effect?

explanation.correct: The default violation mode is 'shutdown': the port is err-disabled on a violation and a notification is sent. You recover it by 'shutdown/no shutdown' (or errdisable recovery).

distractors.B: 'restrict' drops offending frames and sends notifications/increments counters but keeps the port UP (not err-disabled).
distractors.C: 'protect' silently drops offending frames with NO notification.
distractors.D: 'block' is not a port-security violation mode.

explanation.exam_pattern: Violation modes: shutdown (default, err-disable + notify), restrict (drop + notify, stays up), protect (drop silently). Only shutdown err-disables.

questions.stem: After enabling DHCP snooping, clients stop getting addresses from the real DHCP server, which is reached through GigabitEthernet0/24. What is the fix?

options.text: Mark Gi0/24 as a trusted port with 'ip dhcp snooping trust'
Enable 'ip dhcp snooping' on the client access ports only
Add 'ip dhcp snooping limit rate' to Gi0/24

explanation.correct: DHCP snooping treats all ports as untrusted by default and blocks server-sourced messages (OFFER/ACK) on them. The uplink toward the legitimate DHCP server must be set 'ip dhcp snooping trust' so its replies are allowed.

distractors.B: Access ports should stay UNtrusted; trusting them defeats the protection.
distractors.C: Rate-limiting the server uplink would throttle legitimate DHCP, not fix trust.
distractors.D: Disabling snooping removes the protection entirely instead of fixing it.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP snooping: untrusted by default; trust the port(s) toward the real server/uplink. Untrusted ports drop server messages and build the binding table.

questions.stem: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) decides whether an ARP reply is legitimate by checking it against which data source?

explanation.correct: DAI validates ARP packets on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table (IP-to-MAC-to-port). ARPs that don't match a valid binding are dropped, stopping ARP spoofing / man-in-the-middle. DAI therefore depends on DHCP snooping being enabled.

distractors.B: The MAC table only maps MAC→port; it can't confirm the IP/MAC binding DAI needs.
distractors.C: CDP is a discovery protocol, unrelated to ARP validation.
distractors.D: The routing table has no per-host IP-to-MAC binding information.

explanation.exam_pattern: DAI → DHCP snooping binding table; trust uplinks/DHCP ports. DAI stops ARP poisoning; it requires DHCP snooping first.

questions.stem: In an IEEE 802.1X deployment, which device plays the role of the 'authenticator'?

options.text: The LAN switch the client connects to
The end-user PC running the supplicant

explanation.correct: 802.1X has three roles: the supplicant (client software on the PC), the authenticator (the switch/AP that controls port access and relays EAP), and the authentication server (RADIUS, e.g. ISE). The switch is the authenticator.

distractors.B: The PC is the supplicant, not the authenticator.
distractors.C: The RADIUS server is the authentication server.
distractors.D: DHCP plays no role in 802.1X authentication.

explanation.exam_pattern: 802.1X trio: Supplicant (client) ↔ Authenticator (switch/AP) ↔ Authentication server (RADIUS). EAP between supplicant/authenticator, RADIUS behind it.

questions.stem: Which AAA protocol is an open standard that encrypts ONLY the password in the access-request and combines authentication and authorization?

explanation.correct: RADIUS is an open standard (UDP) that encrypts only the password in its packets and merges authentication and authorization into one exchange. It's the usual choice for 802.1X network access.

distractors.B: TACACS+ is Cisco-originated (TCP 49), encrypts the ENTIRE payload, and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting — favored for device administration.
distractors.C: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication system, not the AAA network-access protocol described.
distractors.D: LDAP is a directory-access protocol, not an AAA transport with this behavior.

explanation.exam_pattern: RADIUS: open, UDP, password-only encryption, auth+authz combined (network access). TACACS+: Cisco, TCP 49, full encryption, AAA separated (device admin).

questions.stem: Which IPsec protocol provides confidentiality (encryption) of the data payload?

explanation.correct: ESP (IP protocol 50) provides encryption/confidentiality and optional integrity for the payload. It's what makes IPsec tunnels private.

distractors.B: AH (IP protocol 51) provides integrity/authentication only — no encryption.
distractors.C: IKE negotiates keys/SAs; it sets up protection but ESP does the payload encryption.
distractors.D: GRE is a tunneling protocol with NO native encryption (often paired with IPsec).

explanation.exam_pattern: ESP = encryption (+optional auth). AH = auth only (no encryption). IKE = key management. GRE = tunnel, no crypto by itself.

questions.stem: Which feature err-disables a PortFast edge port the instant it receives a spanning-tree BPDU (e.g., someone plugs in a rogue switch)?

explanation.correct: BPDU Guard shuts (err-disables) a PortFast edge port the moment it receives any BPDU, since edge ports should connect only end hosts. This stops accidental or malicious switches from affecting STP.

distractors.B: Root Guard blocks a port if a superior BPDU would make a neighbor the root; it doesn't err-disable on any BPDU.
distractors.C: Loop Guard prevents a blocking port from wrongly moving to forwarding when BPDUs stop arriving — the opposite trigger.
distractors.D: Storm control limits broadcast/multicast/unicast rates, not BPDUs.

explanation.exam_pattern: BPDU Guard = any BPDU on a PortFast port → err-disable. Root Guard = block superior BPDUs (protect root). Loop Guard = protect against missing BPDUs.

questions.stem: Which configuration is the recommended mitigation against VLAN hopping via the native VLAN?

options.text: Set the trunk native VLAN to an unused VLAN and avoid VLAN 1
Enable DTP dynamic desirable on all access ports

explanation.correct: Changing the native VLAN to a dedicated unused VLAN (and not using VLAN 1 for user data) reduces native-VLAN double-tagging hopping. Hardcoding access/trunk modes and disabling DTP on access ports further hardens it.

distractors.B: Enabling DTP on access ports invites trunk negotiation attacks — the opposite of hardening.
distractors.C: Leaving everything in VLAN 1 is exactly the weak default to avoid.
distractors.D: Disabling BPDU Guard weakens edge security; it doesn't address VLAN hopping.

explanation.exam_pattern: Anti-VLAN-hopping: change native VLAN (unused, not 1), disable DTP ('switchport nonegotiate'), explicitly set access vs trunk, prune allowed VLANs.

questions.stem: Which HTTP method is used by a REST API to RETRIEVE a resource without changing it?

explanation.correct: GET retrieves a representation of a resource and is safe/idempotent — it does not modify server state.

distractors.B: POST creates a new resource (or triggers an action).
distractors.C: DELETE removes a resource.
distractors.D: PUT replaces/updates a resource.

explanation.exam_pattern: CRUD→HTTP: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE. GET is the safe read.

questions.stem: A REST call returns HTTP status code 401. What does that mean?

options.text: Unauthorized — authentication is missing or invalid
The server had an internal error

explanation.correct: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacked valid authentication credentials (or the token expired). Supply/renew credentials and retry.

distractors.B: A successful creation returns 201 Created.
distractors.C: An internal server error is 500.
distractors.D: Not found is 404.

explanation.exam_pattern: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 4xx client error (400 bad, 401 auth, 403 forbidden, 404 not found), 5xx server error (500).

questions.stem: In JSON, how is an ordered list of values represented?

explanation.correct: JSON arrays use square brackets [ ] with comma-separated values. Objects use curly braces { } containing "key": value pairs.

distractors.B: Curly braces denote an OBJECT (key/value pairs), not a bare list.
distractors.C: Dash-prefixed indentation is YAML list syntax, not JSON.
distractors.D: Angle brackets are XML tags.

explanation.exam_pattern: JSON: {} object, [] array, "key":value, strings quoted, true/false/null/numbers. Compare with YAML (indentation, dashes) and XML (tags).

questions.stem: Given the JSON {"interface":{"name":"Gi0/1","enabled":true,"vlans":[10,20]}}, which statement is TRUE?

options.text: 'vlans' is an array with two numeric elements
'enabled' is a string with the value "true"

explanation.correct: 'vlans':[10,20] is a JSON array holding two numbers. 'interface' is an object, 'name' is a string, and 'enabled':true is a boolean (no quotes).

distractors.B: true without quotes is a boolean, not a string.
distractors.C: 'interface' maps to { } — an object, not an array.
distractors.D: "Gi0/1" is quoted, so it's a string, not a number.

explanation.exam_pattern: Read JSON types: {}=object, []=array, ""=string, true/false=bool, bare digits=number. Exam loves 'is enabled a string or boolean?'.

questions.stem: Which configuration-management tool is agentless, pushes configuration over SSH, and uses YAML 'playbooks'?

explanation.correct: Ansible is agentless (connects over SSH/API), uses a PUSH model, and describes desired state in YAML playbooks that are idempotent.

distractors.B: Puppet uses an agent and a PULL model, with manifests in its own declarative DSL (Ruby-based).
distractors.C: Chef uses an agent and PULL model, with recipes/cookbooks in a Ruby DSL.
distractors.D: SaltStack commonly uses minions (agents); Ansible is the agentless/YAML answer here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ansible = agentless, push, YAML. Puppet/Chef = agent, pull (manifests/recipes). Match tool → agent model → language.

questions.stem: Which statement about NETCONF is correct?

options.text: It runs over SSH (port 830) and encodes data in XML using RPCs
It runs over HTTP/HTTPS using REST verbs and JSON only
It is a Cisco-proprietary CLI-scraping protocol
It uses SNMP OIDs to write configuration

explanation.correct: NETCONF uses SSH (TCP 830), exchanges XML-encoded RPCs, works on YANG data models, and supports datastores (running, candidate, startup) with transactional edits.

distractors.B: That describes RESTCONF (HTTP/HTTPS, REST verbs, JSON or XML), not NETCONF.
distractors.C: NETCONF is an IETF standard, not CLI screen-scraping.
distractors.D: NETCONF uses YANG/XML, not SNMP OIDs.

explanation.exam_pattern: NETCONF: SSH 830, XML, RPC, datastores. RESTCONF: HTTP(S), REST verbs, JSON/XML. Both are YANG-model driven.

questions.stem: In an SDN architecture, what does the controller's SOUTHBOUND interface communicate with?

options.text: The network devices (e.g., via NETCONF/OpenFlow) to program the data plane
The business applications requesting network services

explanation.correct: Southbound interfaces (SBIs) run from the controller DOWN to the network devices (using NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, etc.) to program their forwarding. Northbound interfaces (NBIs) face UP to applications.

distractors.B: Applications talk to the controller over the NORTHBOUND interface.
distractors.C: DNS/DHCP are network services, not the SDN SBI target.
distractors.D: End-user browsers aren't part of the controller's programmatic interfaces.

explanation.exam_pattern: Northbound = to apps (REST APIs). Southbound = to devices (NETCONF/OpenFlow). Controller centralizes the control plane.

questions.stem: What does it mean that automation tools aim to be 'idempotent'?

options.text: Re-running the same configuration yields the same end state without duplicate changes
Every run reboots the device to apply changes
Configuration can only be applied once, ever
Each run randomizes the device configuration

explanation.correct: Idempotency means applying the same desired-state definition repeatedly converges to the same result: if the device already matches, nothing changes, so re-runs are safe.

distractors.B: Idempotent tools change only what's needed; they don't force reboots.
distractors.C: You can apply it many times; that's the point — repeatable without side effects.
distractors.D: The opposite — the end state is deterministic, not random.

explanation.exam_pattern: Idempotent = same input → same end state, safe to re-run. Core to Ansible/Puppet/Chef declarative models.

questions.stem: What is the primary benefit of separating the control plane from the data plane in SDN?

options.text: Centralized, programmable control of forwarding across many devices
Eliminating the need for any physical switches
Removing the need for IP addressing
Guaranteeing zero packet loss at all times

explanation.correct: Centralizing the control plane in a controller lets you program and view forwarding policy for the whole fabric from one place (via APIs), improving consistency, automation, and agility.

distractors.B: Physical devices still forward packets (the data plane); SDN doesn't remove them.
distractors.C: IP addressing is still required.
distractors.D: SDN improves control, not a magical zero-loss guarantee.

explanation.exam_pattern: SDN value = centralized/programmable control plane, consistent policy, automation via northbound APIs. Data plane still forwards.

questions.stem: RESTCONF retrieves and modifies configuration modeled in which data-modeling language?

explanation.correct: Both NETCONF and RESTCONF operate on YANG data models, which define the structure of configuration and operational data in a vendor-neutral way.

distractors.B: SQL is for relational databases, not device data models.
distractors.C: ASN.1 defines SNMP MIBs — a different management stack.
distractors.D: HTML is for web documents, not network data modeling.

explanation.exam_pattern: NETCONF + RESTCONF ride on YANG models. RESTCONF = REST over HTTP(S) with JSON/XML; NETCONF = RPC over SSH with XML.

questions.stem: What is the network (subnet) address for the host 192.168.1.200/28?

explanation.correct: A /28 is 255.255.255.240, block size 16: .0, .16, … .192, .208. The host .200 falls in the .192 block (range .192–.207), so the network address is 192.168.1.192.

distractors.B: .200 is a usable host inside the block, not the network address.
distractors.C: .208 is the NEXT subnet's network address.
distractors.D: .196 is not a /28 boundary (boundaries are multiples of 16).

explanation.exam_pattern: Block size 256 − mask octet. Round the host octet DOWN to the nearest multiple of the block size to get the network address.

questions.stem: How many /28 subnets can be created from a single 192.168.5.0/24 network? Enter the number.

explanation.correct: Going from /24 to /28 borrows 4 bits (28 − 24). 2^4 = 16 subnets, each with 14 usable hosts.
explanation.exam_pattern: Number of subnets = 2^(borrowed bits). Borrowed = new prefix − old prefix. /24→/28 borrows 4 → 16 subnets.

questions.stem: Which address block is private (RFC 1918) and must be translated before use on the public Internet?

distractors.B: 172.32.x is OUTSIDE the /12 (which stops at 172.31) and is public.
distractors.C: 11.0.0.0/8 is public address space.
distractors.D: 192.0.2.0/24 is TEST-NET-1 (documentation), not RFC 1918 private.

questions.stem: A PC shows IP address 169.254.13.7 with mask 255.255.0.0. What does this indicate?

options.text: APIPA — the host failed to obtain an address from DHCP
A valid public address was assigned
The host is using a static RFC 1918 address

explanation.correct: 169.254.0.0/16 is the APIPA (link-local) range a host self-assigns when no DHCP server answers. It signals a DHCP problem — the PC can only reach other APIPA hosts on the same segment.

distractors.B: 169.254.x is link-local, not a routable public address.
distractors.C: APIPA is auto-assigned on DHCP failure, not a configured RFC 1918 address.
distractors.D: This is an IPv4 address; IPv6 link-local is FE80::/10.

explanation.exam_pattern: 169.254.x.x (APIPA) = DHCP failed. Check the DHCP server/relay and the path to it.

questions.stem: Which ICMPv6 message does a host receive to learn the on-link prefix and default gateway for stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC)?

explanation.correct: Routers send Router Advertisements (ICMPv6 type 134), which carry the prefix and flags a host uses for SLAAC and to learn its default gateway. Hosts can also prompt one with a Router Solicitation.

distractors.B: Neighbor Solicitation is for address resolution / duplicate address detection, not prefix learning.
distractors.C: DHCPv6 is stateful addressing; SLAAC specifically uses RAs.
distractors.D: A Redirect tells a host of a better next hop, not the SLAAC prefix.

explanation.exam_pattern: SLAAC = Router Advertisement (prefix + gateway) + EUI-64/random host bits. NDP uses NS/NA for resolution, RS/RA for routers.

questions.stem: An Ethernet link is intermittently slow; one side shows increasing late collisions and FCS errors. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A duplex mismatch (one side full-duplex, the other half-duplex)

explanation.correct: Late collisions and FCS/alignment errors on a modern link are the classic signature of a duplex mismatch: the half-duplex side runs CSMA/CD while the full-duplex side transmits whenever it wants, causing collisions detected late. Fix by matching duplex (or both auto).

distractors.B: A VLAN mismatch causes connectivity/segmentation issues, not late collisions.
distractors.C: An MTU mismatch causes drops of oversized frames, not collisions.
distractors.D: A wrong gateway affects routing reachability, not physical collisions.

explanation.exam_pattern: Late collisions + FCS errors = duplex mismatch. Set both ends to auto/auto or hardcode BOTH to the same duplex.

questions.stem: A switch is in 'store-and-forward' switching mode. What does it do before forwarding a frame?

options.text: Receives the entire frame and verifies the FCS before forwarding
Forwards after reading only the first 6 bytes (destination MAC)
Never checks the frame for errors

explanation.correct: Store-and-forward buffers the whole frame and checks the FCS, so corrupt frames are dropped rather than propagated. It adds a little latency but guarantees error-free forwarding (and is required for QoS/different speeds).

distractors.B: Reading only the destination MAC then forwarding is cut-through (fast-forward), which doesn't verify the FCS.
distractors.C: Forwarding after 64 bytes is fragment-free (checks for collision fragments) — a cut-through variant.
distractors.D: Store-and-forward specifically DOES check for errors.

explanation.exam_pattern: Store-and-forward = whole frame + FCS check (error-free, more latency). Cut-through = forward on dest MAC (fast, no FCS check). Fragment-free = first 64 bytes.

questions.stem: Which TCP mechanism lets a receiver control how much data a sender transmits before requiring an acknowledgment?

explanation.correct: TCP flow control uses the window size: the receiver advertises how many bytes it can accept, so the sender can have that much data outstanding before needing an ACK. The window grows/shrinks to match the receiver's capacity.

distractors.B: Sequence numbers order bytes and enable retransmission, not flow control sizing.
distractors.C: The urgent pointer marks urgent data; it isn't flow control.
distractors.D: The checksum verifies integrity, not how much data may be in flight.

explanation.exam_pattern: TCP flow control = sliding window (window size). Reliability = seq/ack + retransmit. Don't confuse windowing with sequencing.

questions.stem: An IP phone with a PC attached behind it connects to one switch port. Which configuration carries PC data on VLAN 10 and phone traffic on VLAN 20?

options.text: switchport access vlan 10 + switchport voice vlan 20
switchport trunk native vlan 10 + allowed vlan 20
switchport access vlan 10 + switchport access vlan 20

explanation.correct: An access port can carry a data VLAN plus a dedicated voice VLAN: 'switchport access vlan 10' for the PC and 'switchport voice vlan 20' for the phone. The phone tags its voice traffic with VLAN 20 while the PC's traffic stays untagged on VLAN 10.

distractors.B: A native-VLAN trunk is not how a phone+PC port is normally built; the voice-VLAN feature is purpose-made for this.
distractors.C: You can't set two access VLANs; the second overwrites the first.
distractors.D: DTP/trunk negotiation isn't needed or appropriate for a host/phone access port.

explanation.exam_pattern: Phone + PC on one port = access vlan (data) + voice vlan. The phone tags voice; the PC is untagged.

questions.stem: Which command disables Dynamic Trunking Protocol so a port will never negotiate a trunk?

explanation.correct: 'switchport nonegotiate' stops the port from sending DTP frames, so it won't dynamically form a trunk. It's a best practice on hardcoded access or trunk ports to prevent DTP-based attacks.

distractors.B: 'dynamic auto' keeps DTP ON (and willing to trunk if asked).
distractors.C: 'no switchport' makes the port a Layer 3 routed port — a different thing.
distractors.D: That's not a valid way to disable negotiation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Harden trunks/access ports: set mode explicitly (access/trunk) AND 'switchport nonegotiate' to kill DTP.

questions.stem: You run 'spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary' on a switch. What priority does it set for VLAN 1 (assuming no other switch is already lower)?

explanation.correct: 'root primary' lowers the bridge priority to 24576 (base 24576 + sys-id-ext). If a rival is already below that, IOS instead sets a value 4096 lower than the current root to win.

distractors.B: 32768 is the DEFAULT priority, not the 'root primary' value.
distractors.C: 4096 is the priority increment/step, not the primary value.
distractors.D: 0 is the lowest configurable priority but not what 'root primary' sets by default.

explanation.exam_pattern: root primary → 24576; root secondary → 28672. Priorities must be multiples of 4096. Lowest bridge ID wins.

questions.stem: In 802.1D STP, which port state learns MAC addresses but does NOT yet forward data frames?

explanation.correct: In the Learning state the switch populates its MAC table from received frames but still does not forward data — the last step before Forwarding.

distractors.B: Listening processes BPDUs but does NOT learn MACs yet.
distractors.C: Forwarding both learns and forwards.
distractors.D: Blocking only listens to BPDUs; it neither learns nor forwards.

explanation.exam_pattern: 802.1D states: Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding (Disabled aside). Learning = builds MAC table, no data forwarding.

questions.stem: An EtherChannel bundles two 1 Gbps links, but one host-to-host transfer never exceeds ~1 Gbps. Why?

options.text: A single flow is hashed to one member link; load-balancing is per-flow, not per-packet by default
EtherChannel only ever uses one link at a time
The channel negotiated down to 100 Mbps
LACP caps throughput at 1 Gbps total

explanation.correct: EtherChannel load-balances per flow using a hash (of MACs/IPs/ports). A single conversation hashes to ONE member, so it's limited to that link's speed. Aggregate bandwidth helps across many flows, not one.

distractors.B: All member links are usable — just not for a single flow.
distractors.C: There's no speed renegotiation implied here.
distractors.D: LACP doesn't impose a 1 Gbps aggregate cap; the limit is per-flow hashing.

explanation.exam_pattern: EtherChannel = per-FLOW hashing. One conversation = one link. Tune 'port-channel load-balance' to spread flows better.

questions.stem: By default, how often does a Cisco device send CDP advertisements, and how long does a neighbor hold the information?

explanation.correct: CDP defaults: advertisements every 60 seconds, hold time 180 seconds (three missed updates before aging out a neighbor).

distractors.B: 30/90 are the LLDP-ish defaults people confuse; CDP is 60/180.
distractors.C: 10/40 are OSPF broadcast hello/dead timers, not CDP.
distractors.D: 90/270 is not the CDP default.

explanation.exam_pattern: CDP timers: 60 s updates, 180 s hold. LLDP defaults: 30 s updates, 120 s hold. Hold is usually 3× the update interval.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between an autonomous AP and a lightweight AP?

options.text: An autonomous AP is self-contained; a lightweight AP is controlled by a WLC
An autonomous AP must be managed by a WLC
A lightweight AP cannot serve clients
They are identical except for color

explanation.correct: An autonomous AP holds its full configuration locally and operates standalone. A lightweight AP offloads control-plane functions to a WLC via CAPWAP (split-MAC), which centralizes management, RF, and mobility.

distractors.B: Reversed — the autonomous AP needs no controller.
distractors.C: Lightweight APs absolutely serve clients; the WLC just controls them.
distractors.D: The architectural difference is real and exam-relevant.

explanation.exam_pattern: Autonomous = standalone config. Lightweight = WLC-controlled via CAPWAP (split-MAC). Centralized vs. independent management.

questions.stem: On a WLC, you want a guest SSID with no encryption but a web page that prompts users to accept terms. Which Layer 3 security should the WLAN use?

explanation.correct: Web authentication (a Layer 3 security option) presents a captive portal — web consent/passthrough for a terms page, or web auth for credentials — which is the usual guest-access pattern on a WLC.

distractors.B: WPA2-Enterprise requires 802.1X credentials/RADIUS, not a simple guest consent page.
distractors.C: WEP is obsolete/insecure and isn't a captive-portal mechanism.
distractors.D: MAC filtering restricts devices but doesn't present a consent page.

explanation.exam_pattern: Guest captive portal = Layer 3 Web Auth (consent/passthrough or credentialed). Enterprise auth = 802.1X (Layer 2).

questions.stem: On a multi-access Ethernet segment, why is a static route configured with only an exit interface (no next-hop IP) problematic?

options.text: The router must ARP for every destination, since it can't resolve a single next hop on a broadcast link
Exit-interface routes are not supported on Ethernet at all
It forces the route's administrative distance to 255

explanation.correct: On a broadcast multi-access link, an interface-only static route makes the router treat every destination as directly connected, so it ARPs for each one (relying on proxy ARP). Specifying a next-hop IP (or both) lets it resolve a single next hop properly.

distractors.B: They ARE supported, but are best used on point-to-point links, not multi-access.
distractors.C: It does not change the AD to 255.
distractors.D: It doesn't disable proxy ARP; it actually depends on it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Point-to-point → exit interface is fine. Multi-access/Ethernet → prefer a next-hop IP (or next-hop + interface) to avoid per-destination ARP.

explanation.correct: Four consecutive /24s combine by borrowing 2 bits back (2^2 = 4), giving a /22. 192.168.0.0/22 covers 192.168.0.0–192.168.3.255 — exactly those four networks.

distractors.B: /23 covers only two /24s (0 and 1).
distractors.C: /21 covers eight /24s (0–7) — too broad.
distractors.D: /24 is just the first network.

explanation.exam_pattern: Summarize 2^n consecutive networks by moving the mask n bits left. 4 networks → /22. Verify the range matches exactly.

questions.stem: Two directly connected OSPF routers never become neighbors (they don't even appear in 'show ip ospf neighbor'). Which mismatch causes this?

options.text: Mismatched hello/dead timers (or area, subnet, or authentication)

explanation.correct: Neighbors never forming (not even showing up) points to a hello-packet parameter mismatch: hello/dead timers, area ID, primary subnet/mask, or authentication must all match to start an adjacency.

distractors.B: An MTU mismatch lets them SEE each other but stick in EXSTART/EXCHANGE — a different symptom.
distractors.C: Reference bandwidth only affects cost/metric, not neighbor formation.
distractors.D: Process IDs are locally significant and need not match.

explanation.exam_pattern: No neighbor at all = hello mismatch (timers/area/subnet/auth). Seen but stuck EXSTART = MTU. Different failure, different cause.

questions.stem: What is the default OSPF network type on an Ethernet interface, and what does it imply?

options.text: Broadcast — a DR and BDR are elected
Non-broadcast — neighbors must be statically defined
Point-to-multipoint — treats each neighbor as a /32

explanation.correct: Ethernet defaults to the OSPF broadcast network type, which elects a DR and BDR to reduce adjacencies and LSA flooding on the shared segment. Hello/dead timers are 10/40 seconds.

distractors.B: Point-to-point (no DR/BDR) is the default on serial/P2P links, with 10/40 timers too but no election.
distractors.C: Non-broadcast (NBMA) is used on legacy Frame Relay and needs manual neighbors.
distractors.D: Point-to-multipoint is a manual type for hub-and-spoke, not the Ethernet default.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ethernet = broadcast (DR/BDR, 10/40). Serial P2P = point-to-point (no DR, 10/40). Change with 'ip ospf network ...'.

questions.stem: OSPF has two paths to the same destination with equal cost. By default, what does the router do?

options.text: Installs both and load-balances (up to the maximum-paths limit, default 4)
Installs only one and ignores the other
Picks the path with the lower administrative distance
Alternates one packet per path regardless of hashing

explanation.correct: OSPF performs equal-cost multipath (ECMP): it installs all equal-cost paths (default 'maximum-paths 4') and load-balances across them, typically per-destination with CEF.

distractors.B: Equal-cost paths are both used, not discarded.
distractors.C: AD is the same (both OSPF); cost is equal, so both install.
distractors.D: CEF usually load-balances per-flow/destination, not strict per-packet.

explanation.exam_pattern: Equal cost → ECMP up to maximum-paths (default 4, up to 16/32). Unequal-cost load balancing is an EIGRP feature (variance), not OSPF.

questions.stem: Enter the command that creates an IPv6 default route toward next hop 2001:DB8::1.

explanation.correct: The IPv6 default route is ::/0 (match anything), pointing to the next hop: 'ipv6 route ::/0 2001:DB8::1'. Remember 'ipv6 unicast-routing' must be enabled for the router to forward IPv6.
explanation.exam_pattern: IPv6 default = ipv6 route ::/0 <next-hop|interface>. IPv4 default = ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop>.

questions.stem: Which statement about VRRP is correct?

options.text: It is an open standard; the master owns the virtual IP and backups take over on failure
It is Cisco-proprietary and uses active/standby terminology
It load-balances across all routers by default like GLBP

explanation.correct: VRRP is an IETF open standard (RFC 5798). One router is elected master (forwards for the virtual IP); others are backups that take over if the master fails. Its virtual MAC is 0000.5E00.01xx.

distractors.B: Active/standby terminology and Cisco-proprietary status describe HSRP, not VRRP.
distractors.C: Plain VRRP is not load-balancing; GLBP provides per-host load balancing.
distractors.D: 0000.0C07.ACxx is HSRP's virtual MAC; VRRP uses 0000.5E00.01xx.

explanation.exam_pattern: HSRP = Cisco, active/standby, 0000.0C07.ACxx. VRRP = open, master/backup, 0000.5E00.01xx. GLBP = Cisco, load-balancing (AVG/AVF).

questions.stem: The same prefix 10.5.0.0/16 is available via a static route (default AD) and via OSPF. Which is installed in the routing table?

options.text: The static route (AD 1), because it is lower than OSPF (AD 110)
The OSPF route, because OSPF is dynamic

explanation.correct: For the same prefix, the lowest administrative distance wins. A static route defaults to AD 1, far below OSPF's 110, so the static route is installed.

distractors.B: Being dynamic doesn't help; AD decides, and static (1) < OSPF (110).
distractors.C: Routes from different sources don't load-balance together.
distractors.D: There's no conflict — AD resolves it cleanly.

explanation.exam_pattern: Same prefix → lowest AD wins. Connected 0, static 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110. A static can shadow a dynamic route unless you raise its AD.

questions.stem: A host can reach devices on its own subnet but nothing beyond it. Pings to the local gateway succeed. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: The host's default gateway is set, but the gateway lacks a route (or return route) to the remote network
The host has no IP address
The switch has a duplex mismatch

explanation.correct: Local connectivity plus a reachable gateway means the host side is fine. Failing to reach remote networks points to the ROUTER: a missing route to the destination, or (commonly) a missing RETURN route back to the host's subnet.

distractors.B: With no IP it couldn't reach the local subnet or ping the gateway.
distractors.C: A duplex mismatch would cause errors/slowness on the link, not a clean 'local works, remote fails' pattern.
distractors.D: A /32 mask would break local connectivity too, which works here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Local OK + gateway reachable + remote fails = routing problem on the router (forward or RETURN route). Always check both directions.

questions.stem: Which wildcard mask in an ACL matches ALL odd-numbered hosts? (Trick: which matches only hosts where the last octet's low bit is set is NOT possible with a simple wildcard — so which statement is TRUE about wildcard masks?)

options.text: A wildcard bit of 1 means 'ignore'; a 0 means 'must match' — they need not be contiguous
Wildcard masks must be the exact inverse of a subnet mask
A wildcard of 0.0.0.255 matches a single host
Wildcard bits of 0 mean 'ignore this bit'

explanation.correct: In a wildcard mask, a 1-bit means 'don't care' (ignore) and a 0-bit means 'must match exactly'. Unlike subnet masks, wildcard bits need not be contiguous, which allows non-contiguous matches (e.g., odd/even hosts with 0.0.0.254 matching even, 0.0.0.254 with base .1 matching odd).

distractors.B: They OFTEN mirror a subnet mask, but wildcard bits can be non-contiguous, so they are not required to be a clean inverse.
distractors.C: 0.0.0.255 matches a whole /24 (256 addresses), not one host (that's 0.0.0.0 / 'host').
distractors.D: Reversed — a 0 bit means 'must match', a 1 bit means 'ignore'.

explanation.exam_pattern: Wildcard: 0 = match, 1 = ignore. Bits can be non-contiguous. 'host' = 0.0.0.0, 'any' = 255.255.255.255.

questions.stem: In NAT terminology, what is the 'inside local' address?

options.text: The private IP of an inside host as seen inside the network
The public IP an inside host is translated to
The public IP of an outside host
The private IP of an outside host

explanation.correct: Inside local = the inside host's address as used INSIDE the network (usually its private IP). After translation it becomes the inside global (the public address seen outside).

distractors.B: The translated public address of an inside host is the inside GLOBAL.
distractors.C: An outside host's public address is the outside global.
distractors.D: An outside host's address as seen inside is the outside local.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inside = your host; Outside = their host. Local = as seen on the inside; Global = as seen on the outside. Inside local → inside global is the usual translation.

questions.stem: Enter the global command that configures a router to synchronize its clock from an NTP server at 10.0.0.1.

explanation.correct: 'ntp server 10.0.0.1' points the device at that NTP source. Verify with 'show ntp associations' (a '*' marks the synchronized peer) and 'show ntp status'.
explanation.exam_pattern: Client: 'ntp server <ip>'. Local authoritative source: 'ntp master <stratum>'. Accurate time matters for logs, certs, and Kerberos.

questions.stem: On an IOS DHCP server, which command prevents the pool from handing out 10.0.0.1 through 10.0.0.9 (reserved for infrastructure)?

explanation.correct: 'ip dhcp excluded-address 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.9' (a global command) removes that range from any pool's assignable addresses, protecting gateways, servers, and printers.

distractors.B: There is no 'exclude' keyword inside the pool for this.
distractors.C: 'ip dhcp reserved' is not the exclusion command.
distractors.D: Invalid syntax; the pool's 'network' defines the scope, not exclusions.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reserve addresses with the GLOBAL 'ip dhcp excluded-address <start> <end>' before defining the pool's network.

questions.stem: In SNMPv2c, what is the difference between an RO and an RW community string?

options.text: RO allows only reads (GET); RW also allows writes (SET) to change device config/state
RO is encrypted; RW is plaintext
RO uses port 161; RW uses port 162

explanation.correct: A read-only (RO) community permits GET operations to read values; a read-write (RW) community additionally permits SET operations that change configuration/state. Both are sent in clear text in v2c, which is why v3 is preferred.

distractors.B: Neither is encrypted in v2c; the strings are plaintext.
distractors.C: Polling is 161 and traps 162 regardless of RO/RW.
distractors.D: The read-only vs read-write capability is a real, important difference.

explanation.exam_pattern: v2c: RO = read, RW = read+write (dangerous if exposed). No encryption → prefer SNMPv3 (authPriv).

questions.stem: Which pair of commands sends log messages of severity 'warnings' and more severe to a syslog server at 10.1.1.50?

explanation.correct: 'logging host 10.1.1.50' (or 'logging 10.1.1.50') names the server and 'logging trap warnings' (level 4) sets the minimum severity sent — warnings and anything more severe (0–4).

distractors.B: 'logging console' controls console output, not a remote host; 'logging level' isn't the trap command.
distractors.C: 'snmp-server host' is for SNMP traps, not syslog.
distractors.D: 'logging buffered' stores logs locally in RAM, not to a remote server.

explanation.exam_pattern: Remote syslog = 'logging host <ip>' + 'logging trap <severity>'. Severity is a threshold: that level and all MORE severe.

references: CCNA 200-301 Topic 4.5 syslog to a server

questions.stem: A client's DHCP lease is near expiry. At roughly what point does the client first try to RENEW the lease with the original server (unicast)?

explanation.correct: At T1 (50% of the lease) the client unicasts a DHCPREQUEST to renew with the leasing server. If that fails, at T2 (~87.5%) it broadcasts to rebind with any server; at 100% without success it releases the address.

distractors.B: At 100% the lease expires and the client stops using the address if not renewed.
distractors.C: 87.5% is T2 (rebinding, broadcast to any server), which comes after T1.
distractors.D: Renewal timers start counting from the lease, not right after the ACK.

explanation.exam_pattern: Renew at T1 (50%, unicast to server), rebind at T2 (87.5%, broadcast), expire at 100%. DORA to get it, T1/T2 to keep it.

questions.stem: Where should the QoS 'trust boundary' ideally be placed in a campus so that end-user PCs cannot set their own high-priority markings?

options.text: At the access-layer switch port (trust phones/APs, not PCs)
At the core, trusting everything below it
Nowhere — markings should always be trusted

explanation.correct: The trust boundary should be as close to the source as practical — the access switch — where you trust markings from managed devices (IP phones via CDP, APs) but re-mark or ignore markings from untrusted PCs, so users can't claim priority.

distractors.B: Trusting from the core lets untrusted PC markings propagate unchecked up the network.
distractors.C: PCs are exactly what you should NOT trust by default.
distractors.D: Blindly trusting all markings lets anyone grab priority bandwidth.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trust boundary = access edge. Trust phones/APs, condition/ignore PC markings. Classify and mark as close to the source as you can.

questions.stem: Which numbered range identifies an EXTENDED IPv4 ACL?

explanation.correct: Extended IPv4 ACLs use 100–199 (and the expanded 2000–2699). They match protocol, source, destination, and ports.

distractors.B: 1–99 and 1300–1999 are STANDARD ACLs (source only).
distractors.C: 200–299 is used for protocol type-code (Ethernet) ACLs, not extended IP.
distractors.D: 600–699 historically is AppleTalk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Standard = 1–99 / 1300–1999 (source only). Extended = 100–199 / 2000–2699 (proto/src/dst/port). Named ACLs avoid memorizing numbers.

questions.stem: In a NAMED extended ACL, how can you insert a new permit statement BETWEEN two existing entries without rebuilding the ACL?

options.text: Enter the ACL and add the entry with a sequence number between the neighbors' numbers
You cannot; named ACLs must be deleted and recreated
Re-apply the ACL to the interface in reverse

explanation.correct: Named (and modern numbered) ACLs support sequence numbers. Enter the ACL configuration and add a line with a sequence number between the existing ones (e.g., '15 permit ...' between 10 and 20) to place it exactly.

distractors.B: Editing by sequence number is exactly what named ACLs allow.
distractors.C: There is no 'insert' keyword; you use sequence numbers.
distractors.D: Re-applying to the interface doesn't reorder entries.

explanation.exam_pattern: Named/numbered ACLs: edit by sequence number; 'ip access-list resequence' re-spaces them. Order still matters (first match wins).

questions.stem: What does 'switchport port-security mac-address sticky' do?

options.text: Dynamically learns connected MACs and adds them to the running config as secure addresses
Permanently blocks all MAC addresses on the port
Forces the port into err-disabled immediately

explanation.correct: Sticky learning converts dynamically learned MACs into secure entries written to the running configuration, so they survive as allowed addresses (and persist if you save) without typing each one manually.

distractors.B: It allows the learned MACs, not blocks them.
distractors.C: Err-disable happens only on a violation, per the violation mode.
distractors.D: It relies on learning; it doesn't disable it.

explanation.exam_pattern: sticky = learn dynamically, then pin into running-config as secure. Pair with 'maximum <n>' and a violation mode.

questions.stem: Which IOS password storage is WEAK because it is trivially reversible, and so should be avoided for the enable secret?

explanation.correct: Type 7 encryption (what 'service password-encryption' applies) is a weak, easily reversible cipher — it only hides passwords from shoulder-surfing. Use type 8 (PBKDF2) or type 9 (scrypt) for the enable secret.

distractors.B: Type 8 (PBKDF2-SHA256) is a strong one-way hash — recommended.
distractors.C: Type 9 (scrypt) is strong and memory-hard — recommended.
distractors.D: Type 5 (MD5) is a one-way hash, far stronger than type 7 (though 8/9 are preferred now).

explanation.exam_pattern: Type 7 = reversible/weak (service password-encryption). Type 5 = MD5. Type 8 = PBKDF2, Type 9 = scrypt (strongest). Use 'enable secret' with 8/9.

questions.stem: Why is 'enable secret' preferred over 'enable password'?

options.text: 'enable secret' stores a strong one-way hash; 'enable password' is plaintext (or weak type 7)
They are identical; 'secret' is just an alias

explanation.correct: 'enable secret' hashes the privileged-mode password (type 5/8/9), which is far more secure than 'enable password', stored in clear text (or only weak type 7 with service password-encryption). If both exist, 'enable secret' wins.

distractors.B: 'enable password' is not AES-encrypted; it's plaintext/type 7.
distractors.C: They are not identical; the storage security differs greatly.
distractors.D: It doesn't disable the console.

explanation.exam_pattern: Always use 'enable secret' (hashed). 'enable password' is legacy and weak. If both configured, 'enable secret' takes effect.

questions.stem: Given 'aaa authentication login default group radius local', what happens if the RADIUS server is unreachable when a user logs in?

options.text: The device falls back to the LOCAL user database
The user is granted access with no password
RADIUS is retried forever, blocking login

explanation.correct: A method list is tried in order. If 'group radius' is UNREACHABLE (no response), IOS proceeds to the next method, 'local', and authenticates against local accounts. Note: an actual REJECT from RADIUS stops the list (it doesn't fall through).

distractors.B: It isn't denied outright; the next method (local) is used on unreachability.
distractors.C: Fallback still requires valid local credentials, not open access.
distractors.D: It moves on to the next method rather than retrying forever.

explanation.exam_pattern: Method list = ordered fallbacks tried only when a method is UNREACHABLE. A definitive reject ends the list. Always include 'local' as a backstop.

questions.stem: DHCP snooping builds a table of IP-to-MAC-to-port bindings. Which other security feature consumes this table to validate traffic?

options.text: Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard

explanation.correct: The DHCP snooping binding table is the trust source for Dynamic ARP Inspection (validates ARP) and IP Source Guard (validates the source IP/MAC on a port). All three work together to stop spoofing at Layer 2.

distractors.B: PortFast speeds STP edge transitions; it uses no binding table.
distractors.C: CDP is discovery, unrelated to the binding table.
distractors.D: UDLD detects unidirectional fiber links, not spoofing.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP snooping → binding table → DAI (ARP) + IP Source Guard (source IP/MAC). The Layer 2 anti-spoofing trio.

questions.stem: Which VPN type connects two sites' gateways so hosts behind them communicate transparently, without any client software on the hosts?

explanation.correct: A site-to-site IPsec VPN is built between two gateways (routers/firewalls). Hosts behind each site communicate as if directly connected, with the gateways handling encryption — no per-host client needed.

distractors.B: Remote-access VPNs serve individual users/devices with a client.
distractors.C: Clientless web VPN is a remote-access method for a single user via browser.
distractors.D: DMVPN scales site-to-site tunnels but isn't 'per user' client dial-in.

explanation.exam_pattern: Site-to-site = gateway-to-gateway, transparent to hosts. Remote-access = per-user client (AnyConnect/SSL). Match topology to type.

questions.stem: What is the difference between HTTP PUT and PATCH in a REST API?

options.text: PUT replaces the entire resource; PATCH applies a partial update
PUT reads a resource; PATCH deletes it
PUT is unencrypted; PATCH is encrypted

explanation.correct: PUT replaces the whole target resource with the payload (and is idempotent). PATCH modifies only the specified fields — a partial update.

distractors.B: GET reads and DELETE removes; PUT/PATCH both write.
distractors.C: Encryption depends on HTTPS, not the method.
distractors.D: Full-replace vs partial-update is a real difference.

explanation.exam_pattern: CRUD: POST create, GET read, PUT replace (whole), PATCH update (partial), DELETE remove.

questions.stem: Which of the following is VALID JSON?

explanation.correct: Valid JSON uses double-quoted keys and string values, square brackets for arrays, and commas between elements: {"vlans": [10, 20, 30], "name": "access"}.

distractors.B: JSON requires double quotes (not single) and has no tuple '()' type.
distractors.C: Keys/strings must be quoted and array elements comma-separated.
distractors.D: That's XML, not JSON.

explanation.exam_pattern: JSON must use double quotes, [] arrays, {} objects, commas. Single quotes, unquoted keys, or tuples are invalid.

questions.stem: In Ansible, what is a 'playbook'?

options.text: A YAML file describing ordered tasks/desired state to apply to inventory hosts
A compiled binary agent installed on each device
A Python script that must run on each managed node

explanation.correct: An Ansible playbook is a YAML document that lists plays and tasks (using modules) to bring inventory hosts to a desired state. Ansible is agentless and pushes over SSH/API.

distractors.B: Ansible is agentless — no binary agent on devices.
distractors.C: Credentials/variables live in inventory/vault, not 'the playbook' as a definition.
distractors.D: Playbooks run from the control node; they don't execute locally on each device.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ansible playbook = YAML tasks/plays for inventory hosts, agentless, idempotent, pushed over SSH. Inventory lists the hosts.

questions.stem: Why is a webhook (event-driven callback) often more efficient than repeatedly polling a REST API?

options.text: The server pushes a notification only when an event occurs, avoiding constant requests

explanation.correct: A webhook has the server call YOU (an HTTP POST to your endpoint) the moment something changes, so you get timely updates without the wasted requests and latency of polling on an interval.

distractors.B: Webhooks are HTTP callbacks.
distractors.C: Polling can absolutely authenticate.
distractors.D: Both can use HTTPS; encryption isn't the distinction.

explanation.exam_pattern: Polling = client asks repeatedly (wasteful). Webhook = server pushes on event (efficient, timely). Same push vs pull idea as telemetry vs SNMP.

questions.stem: As data moves down the OSI stack from a sending host, what is the correct order of the Protocol Data Units (PDUs)?

explanation.correct: Encapsulation proceeds Data (L5-7) → Segment (L4, TCP/UDP) → Packet (L3, IP) → Frame (L2) → Bits (L1). Each layer adds its header as the PDU goes down the stack.

distractors.B: That's the DE-encapsulation order (receiving side, going up).
distractors.C: Segment (L4) comes before Packet becomes Frame; this order is scrambled.
distractors.D: The L4 Segment must come before the L3 Packet, not after.

explanation.exam_pattern: Down the stack: Data, Segment, Packet, Frame, Bits. L4=segment, L3=packet, L2=frame, L1=bits. Reverse on receive.

questions.stem: A traditional firewall that filters on source/destination IP AND TCP/UDP port numbers operates primarily at which OSI layers?

explanation.correct: Filtering on IP addresses is Layer 3 and on TCP/UDP ports is Layer 4, so a stateful packet-filtering firewall works at Layers 3–4. (Next-gen firewalls add Layer 7 application awareness.)

distractors.B: L1/L2 deal with bits and frames/MACs, not IP/port filtering.
distractors.C: Layer 7 is application content inspection; basic port/IP filtering is L3/L4.
distractors.D: A switch is L2; a port/IP firewall reaches L3/L4.

explanation.exam_pattern: Map the device to layers: switch L2, router/basic-firewall L3(-4), NGFW/proxy L7. IP = L3, ports = L4.

questions.stem: In the four-layer TCP/IP model, which single layer corresponds to the OSI Session, Presentation, and Application layers (5, 6, and 7)?

explanation.correct: The TCP/IP model collapses OSI layers 5–7 into a single Application layer. Its Transport maps to OSI L4, Internet to L3, and Link/Network Access to L1–L2.

distractors.B: Transport maps to OSI Layer 4 only.
distractors.C: Internet maps to OSI Layer 3.
distractors.D: Link/Network Access maps to OSI Layers 1–2.

explanation.exam_pattern: TCP/IP (4): Application (OSI 5-7), Transport (4), Internet (3), Link (1-2). Know the mapping both directions.

questions.stem: Compared with the 2.4 GHz band, what is a key trade-off of the 5 GHz band?

options.text: More non-overlapping channels and higher throughput, but shorter range / less wall penetration
Longer range and better penetration, but fewer channels
Identical range and channels to 2.4 GHz
It cannot be used for Wi-Fi

explanation.correct: 5 GHz offers many more non-overlapping channels and higher data rates with less interference, but its higher frequency means shorter range and weaker penetration through walls than 2.4 GHz.

distractors.B: That describes 2.4 GHz (better range/penetration, only 3 clean channels).
distractors.C: They differ significantly in channels and range.
distractors.D: 5 GHz is widely used for Wi-Fi (802.11a/n/ac/ax).

explanation.exam_pattern: 2.4 GHz = better range/penetration, 3 clean channels (1/6/11), more interference. 5 GHz = more channels/throughput, shorter range.

questions.stem: In wireless terminology, what is an SSID?

options.text: The human-readable name of a wireless network (WLAN)
The MAC address of the access point's radio
The channel number the AP uses
The encryption key for the network

explanation.correct: The SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the network name clients see and join. The AP radio's MAC that identifies a specific basic service set is the BSSID — a different thing.

distractors.B: The radio MAC identifying a BSS is the BSSID, not the SSID.
distractors.C: The channel is an RF setting, not the network name.
distractors.D: The encryption key (PSK) is separate from the SSID.

explanation.exam_pattern: SSID = network NAME. BSSID = AP radio MAC (one BSS). ESS = multiple APs sharing one SSID for roaming.

questions.stem: Which non-Wi-Fi source is a common cause of interference specifically in the 2.4 GHz band?

options.text: Microwave ovens and classic Bluetooth devices

explanation.correct: Microwave ovens and older Bluetooth both operate in the 2.4 GHz ISM band, so they can interfere with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi — one more reason crowded 2.4 GHz is noisier than 5 GHz.

distractors.B: Fiber carries light internally and emits no RF interference.
distractors.C: Copper Ethernet isn't a 2.4 GHz RF source for Wi-Fi.
distractors.D: Optical transceivers don't radiate 2.4 GHz RF.

explanation.exam_pattern: 2.4 GHz interferers: microwaves, Bluetooth, cordless phones, baby monitors. Another reason to prefer 5 GHz where range allows.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes single-mode fiber (SMF) from multimode fiber (MMF)?

options.text: SMF uses a laser and a small core for long distances; MMF uses LED/VCSEL and a larger core for shorter distances
MMF reaches much farther than SMF
SMF carries electrical signals; MMF carries light
They are interchangeable on the same transceivers

explanation.correct: SMF has a very small core and uses a laser to send one light path over long distances (kilometers). MMF has a larger core, uses LED/VCSEL sources, and is used for shorter runs (campus/data center).

distractors.B: SMF reaches much farther than MMF, not the other way around.
distractors.C: Both carry light; neither carries electrical signals.
distractors.D: SMF and MMF require matching optics; they're not interchangeable.

explanation.exam_pattern: SMF = small core, laser, long haul. MMF = large core, LED/VCSEL, shorter. Match the fiber type to the transceiver and distance.

questions.stem: What is the standard maximum cable length for a 1000BASE-T (Gigabit over copper twisted pair) Ethernet run?

explanation.correct: Twisted-pair Ethernet (10/100/1000BASE-T) is specified to 100 meters (about 328 feet) per run. Beyond that you need fiber or a repeater/switch.

distractors.B: 550 m is a multimode-fiber figure, not copper.
distractors.C: 10 m is far below the copper limit.
distractors.D: 1 km is a single-mode-fiber range, not copper.

explanation.exam_pattern: Copper UTP Ethernet = 100 m max. Need more? Use fiber (MMF ~hundreds of m, SMF km). Cat5e/6/6a differ in speed/shielding, not the 100 m.

questions.stem: Which command shows a neighbor's platform, remote port, and management address learned via Cisco Discovery Protocol?

explanation.correct: 'show cdp neighbors detail' lists each directly connected Cisco neighbor's device ID, platform, local and remote interfaces, IOS version, and management IP — great for mapping a topology.

distractors.B: 'show interfaces status' shows local port state/VLAN, not neighbor detail.
distractors.C: 'show ip arp' maps IP↔MAC, not CDP neighbor info.
distractors.D: 'show mac address-table' maps MAC↔port, not neighbor platform/version.

explanation.exam_pattern: CDP/LLDP neighbor detail = device id, local/remote port, platform, mgmt IP. Use the plain 'show cdp neighbors' for a quick summary.

questions.stem: Which protocol extension lets a switch advertise the voice VLAN and PoE/QoS policy to an attached IP phone, even from non-Cisco gear?

explanation.correct: LLDP-MED (Media Endpoint Discovery) extends LLDP to exchange voice-VLAN, power (PoE), and QoS policy with endpoints like IP phones — the open-standard counterpart to Cisco's CDP voice-VLAN signaling.

distractors.B: CDP can do this for Cisco gear, but the question asks for the open standard that also works with non-Cisco phones.
distractors.C: DTP negotiates trunking, not endpoint media policy.
distractors.D: VTP distributes VLAN databases between switches, not endpoint policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: LLDP-MED = voice VLAN + PoE + QoS to endpoints (open). CDP does the same for Cisco. DTP=trunk negotiation, VTP=VLAN DB sync.

questions.stem: A lightweight AP is powered up on a new VLAN but can't find its WLC. Which method is commonly used to tell the AP the controller's IP during CAPWAP discovery?

explanation.correct: DHCP option 43 can return the WLC management IP(s) to a lightweight AP during CAPWAP discovery. APs also try a saved/primed controller, a DNS name (CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER), and local subnet broadcast.

distractors.B: Option 150 is for TFTP servers (e.g., IP phones), not CAPWAP WLC discovery; and it's a DHCP option, not CDP.
distractors.C: STP root ID is unrelated to AP-to-WLC discovery.
distractors.D: A gateway provides routing but doesn't tell the AP the WLC address.

explanation.exam_pattern: CAPWAP WLC discovery: primed/stored, DHCP option 43, DNS (CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER), subnet broadcast. Option 43 is the classic exam answer.

questions.stem: A WLAN is configured to NOT broadcast its SSID. Is this an effective security control?

options.text: No — hiding the SSID is obscurity only; the name is still discoverable, so use WPA2/WPA3 for real security
Yes — a hidden SSID fully encrypts the traffic
Yes — it prevents any device from connecting
No — it disables the radio entirely

explanation.correct: Not broadcasting the SSID only hides the name from casual scans; the SSID still appears in client probe/association frames and is easily recovered. Real protection comes from strong authentication/encryption (WPA2/WPA3), not hiding the name.

distractors.B: Hiding the name does not encrypt anything.
distractors.C: Clients that know the name can still connect.
distractors.D: It doesn't disable the radio; the WLAN still operates.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hidden SSID = obscurity, not security. Rely on WPA2/WPA3 (enterprise/personal). MAC filtering is also weak on its own.

questions.stem: On a Cisco WLC, which interface is used for the controller's own management and typically sources CAPWAP toward the APs?

explanation.correct: The management interface handles in-band controller management and is the usual source/endpoint for CAPWAP control traffic with the APs.

distractors.B: Dynamic interfaces map WLANs to client VLANs, not controller management.
distractors.C: The virtual interface supports web auth, DHCP relay, and mobility — not general management.
distractors.D: The redundancy port is for WLC HA pairing, not AP management.

explanation.exam_pattern: WLC interfaces: management (control/CAPWAP), virtual (web-auth/DHCP/mobility), dynamic (client VLANs), service (OOB). Know each role.

questions.stem: When does an IPv4 host send a packet to its default gateway rather than delivering it directly?

options.text: When the destination is on a DIFFERENT subnet than the host
When the destination is on the SAME subnet
For every packet, local or remote

explanation.correct: A host ANDs the destination IP with its own mask: if the destination is on a different subnet, it forwards the frame to the default gateway (the router) to be routed. Same-subnet traffic is delivered directly via ARP.

distractors.B: Same-subnet traffic goes directly to the host, not the gateway.
distractors.C: Local traffic bypasses the gateway.
distractors.D: Broadcasts stay on the local subnet; they aren't sent to the gateway to route.

explanation.exam_pattern: Host logic: same subnet → ARP + deliver directly; different subnet → send to default gateway. The gateway must be ON the host's subnet.

questions.stem: In 'show ip route', a router prints 'Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0'. What does this mean?

options.text: Packets that match no more-specific route are forwarded to 203.0.113.1 (the default route next hop)
The router has no routes at all

explanation.correct: The gateway of last resort is where the router sends traffic that matches no specific route — i.e., the next hop of the default route (0.0.0.0/0). Here that's 203.0.113.1.

distractors.B: It has at least a default route; more-specific routes may also exist.
distractors.C: 203.0.113.1 is the default next hop, not necessarily a loopback.
distractors.D: Unmatched traffic is forwarded to that next hop, not dropped.

explanation.exam_pattern: Gateway of last resort = default-route next hop. 'No gateway of last resort' means no default and unmatched packets are dropped.

references: CCNA 200-301 Topic 3.1 gateway of last resort

questions.stem: To give hosts a redundant default gateway, what IP address should the hosts use as their gateway when HSRP/VRRP is deployed on two routers?

options.text: The virtual IP address shared by the FHRP group
The physical IP of the primary router
The physical IP of the backup router
The broadcast address of the subnet

explanation.correct: Hosts point to the FHRP virtual IP. Whichever router is active owns that virtual IP/MAC, so if it fails the standby takes over the same virtual address transparently — the hosts never change their gateway.

distractors.B: Using a router's physical IP means losing the gateway if that router fails.
distractors.C: Same problem — a physical IP isn't redundant.
distractors.D: The broadcast address is not a gateway.

explanation.exam_pattern: FHRP (HSRP/VRRP/GLBP): hosts use the VIRTUAL IP. The active router owns it; failover moves the virtual IP/MAC transparently.

questions.stem: A client asks its configured DNS server to fully resolve www.example.com. The server then queries root, TLD, and authoritative servers on the client's behalf. What is this type of lookup called?

options.text: A recursive query (the resolver does the work and returns the final answer)
An iterative query performed by the client

explanation.correct: In a recursive query the client asks its resolver for the final answer, and the resolver does the iterative legwork (root → TLD → authoritative) and returns the result, caching it along the way.

distractors.B: Iterative queries (referrals) are what the resolver uses toward other servers; the client's request to its resolver is recursive.
distractors.C: A PTR lookup resolves IP → name, not this name → IP resolution.
distractors.D: A zone transfer replicates a whole zone between DNS servers.

explanation.exam_pattern: Client→resolver = recursive (give me the answer). Resolver→others = iterative (referrals). Resolver caches results by TTL.

questions.stem: Which DNS record type creates an ALIAS so that one name resolves to another canonical name?

explanation.correct: A CNAME (canonical name) record aliases one name to another — e.g., www.example.com → example.com — so the resolver then looks up the target's A/AAAA record.

distractors.B: An A record maps a name directly to an IPv4 address.
distractors.C: MX points to a mail exchanger for a domain.
distractors.D: NS delegates a zone to authoritative name servers.

explanation.exam_pattern: A = name→IPv4, AAAA = name→IPv6, CNAME = alias→name, MX = mail, NS = delegation, PTR = reverse.

questions.stem: Enter the IOS global command that creates a static hostname-to-IP mapping so 'ping R2' works without DNS, mapping R2 to 10.0.0.2.

explanation.correct: 'ip host R2 10.0.0.2' adds a local static name entry, so the device resolves 'R2' to 10.0.0.2 without a DNS server — handy in labs.
explanation.exam_pattern: Static local names = 'ip host <name> <ip>'. For a DNS server use 'ip name-server' + 'ip domain-lookup'. 'show hosts' lists the cache.

questions.stem: A router has no upstream time source but should serve time to the LAN. Which command makes it an authoritative NTP source at stratum 3?

explanation.correct: 'ntp master 3' makes the device an authoritative NTP server using its own clock, advertising stratum 3. Clients then point to it with 'ntp server <ip>'.

distractors.B: 'ntp server' makes the device a CLIENT of another server.
distractors.C: 'ntp peer' forms a symmetric peer relationship, not a local master.
distractors.D: 'clock stratum' is not a valid IOS command for this.

explanation.exam_pattern: Local authoritative source = 'ntp master <stratum>'. Client = 'ntp server <ip>'. Lower stratum = closer to the reference.

questions.stem: Why does accurate, synchronized time (NTP) matter for network operations?

options.text: Correlating log timestamps across devices, and validating time-sensitive items like certificates and Kerberos tickets
It is required for STP to converge

explanation.correct: Synchronized clocks let you correlate syslog/event timestamps across devices during troubleshooting, and are essential for certificate validity windows, Kerberos, and accurate accounting/logging.

distractors.B: NTP doesn't affect bandwidth.
distractors.C: NTP itself isn't an encryption service (it can be authenticated).
distractors.D: STP convergence doesn't depend on NTP.

explanation.exam_pattern: NTP = consistent time → correlated logs, valid certs/Kerberos, trustworthy accounting. A foundational operational service.

questions.stem: Which SNMP operation does a MANAGER use to retrieve the next object in a MIB tree, enabling a 'walk' of a table?

explanation.correct: GETNEXT returns the next OID/value after the one requested, which lets a manager walk through table rows and discover objects without knowing every index in advance.

distractors.B: SET writes a value to a writable object.
distractors.C: A Trap is an unsolicited notification from the AGENT to the manager.
distractors.D: An Inform is an acknowledged notification from the agent, not a manager read.

explanation.exam_pattern: Manager ops: GET (one), GETNEXT/GETBULK (walk), SET (write). Agent notifications: Trap (no ack), Inform (acked).

questions.stem: Which command configures where an IOS device SENDS SNMP trap notifications?

explanation.correct: 'snmp-server host <ip> ...' defines the trap/inform receiver (the NMS) and the version/community or user to use. 'snmp-server enable traps' chooses which notifications to send.

distractors.B: 'snmp-server community' sets an access string for polling, not the trap destination.
distractors.C: 'logging host' is for SYSLOG, not SNMP traps.
distractors.D: 'snmp-server location' sets descriptive sysLocation only.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trap target = 'snmp-server host' + 'snmp-server enable traps'. Polling access = 'snmp-server community' / v3 user. Syslog is separate.

questions.stem: Given the message '%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down', what does the '3' indicate?

options.text: The number of times it occurred

explanation.correct: In 'FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC', the number is the severity. Here LINK is the facility, 3 is the severity (Error), and UPDOWN is the mnemonic describing the event.

distractors.B: The interface is named in the message text (Gi0/1), not by the 3.
distractors.C: It isn't an occurrence count.
distractors.D: The facility is the text before the number (LINK), not the number itself.

explanation.exam_pattern: Syslog format: %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: text. Severity 0–7 (0=emergency … 7=debug). Lower = more severe.

questions.stem: Which logging destination keeps messages in the device's RAM so you can review recent events with 'show logging', even with no syslog server?

explanation.correct: 'logging buffered [size] [severity]' stores log messages in a RAM buffer, viewable with 'show logging'. It survives until reboot or buffer wrap — handy when there's no syslog server.

distractors.B: Console logging prints to the console session; it isn't a reviewable stored buffer.
distractors.C: A remote host requires a syslog server, which the question excludes.
distractors.D: NVRAM holds the startup config, not the live log buffer.

explanation.exam_pattern: Destinations: console, vty/monitor (terminal monitor), buffered (RAM, 'show logging'), host (remote syslog). Buffer = local history.

questions.stem: On a switch running Dynamic ARP Inspection, how are ports classified by default, and what happens to ARP replies on them?

options.text: All ports are untrusted by default; ARP is validated against the DHCP snooping bindings and dropped if it doesn't match
All ports are trusted by default; ARP is never inspected
DAI inspects only the first ARP per port

explanation.correct: DAI treats ports as untrusted by default and checks each ARP on them against the DHCP snooping binding table (IP↔MAC↔port). Mismatched ARPs are dropped, stopping ARP spoofing.

distractors.B: Trusted-by-default would defeat DAI; untrusted is the safe default.
distractors.C: Access ports toward hosts stay untrusted; uplinks are explicitly trusted.
distractors.D: DAI inspects ARPs continuously, not just the first.

explanation.exam_pattern: DAI: untrusted by default, validate against DHCP snooping bindings, trust uplinks/DHCP-facing ports. Requires DHCP snooping.

questions.stem: Which ports should be configured as DAI 'trusted'?

options.text: Uplinks to other switches / the DHCP server path

explanation.correct: Trust the infrastructure uplinks (switch-to-switch and toward the DHCP server), where legitimate ARPs transit, and keep user access ports untrusted so host ARPs are validated against the bindings.

distractors.B: Trusting user ports would let an attacker spoof ARPs freely.
distractors.C: Uplinks generally must be trusted or valid traffic gets dropped.
distractors.D: VLAN membership isn't the basis for trust; the port's role is.

explanation.exam_pattern: DAI trust = uplinks/DHCP path. Untrusted = user access ports (validated). Same trust pattern as DHCP snooping.

questions.stem: A server uses a STATIC IP (no DHCP), so DAI keeps dropping its ARPs. How do you allow it without disabling DAI?

options.text: Define an ARP ACL mapping the server's IP to its MAC and apply it to DAI for that VLAN
Give the server an APIPA address

explanation.correct: Statically addressed hosts have no DHCP snooping binding, so you create an ARP access-list (IP↔MAC) and apply it to DAI for the VLAN. DAI then permits the server's ARPs while still validating everyone else.

distractors.B: Trusting all access ports removes protection for everyone.
distractors.C: Disabling snooping breaks DAI (which relies on the binding table).
distractors.D: Giving it APIPA breaks its connectivity and doesn't fix ARP validation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Static hosts + DAI = ARP ACL (permit ip host <ip> mac host <mac>) applied to the VLAN. Keeps DAI on for everyone else.

questions.stem: Why does DAI apply a default rate limit to ARP packets on untrusted ports?

options.text: ARP inspection is CPU-based, so a flood could overwhelm the switch; exceeding the rate err-disables the port

explanation.correct: Because DAI validation is done in software (CPU), a burst of ARPs could be a DoS against the switch. A default per-port rate limit on untrusted ports err-disables a port that exceeds it, protecting the control plane.

distractors.B: DAI validates ARP; it doesn't encrypt it.
distractors.C: Rate limiting constrains, not accelerates, ARP.
distractors.D: DAI isn't an addressing mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: DAI rate-limits ARP on untrusted ports (CPU protection); exceed → err-disable. Recover via shutdown/no shutdown or errdisable recovery.

questions.stem: Enter the interface command that limits a port-security-enabled port to a maximum of 2 learned MAC addresses.

explanation.correct: 'switchport port-security maximum 2' caps the number of secure MAC addresses on the port at 2 (e.g., a PC plus a phone). A new MAC beyond the max triggers the violation action.
explanation.exam_pattern: port-security building blocks: 'switchport port-security' (enable) + 'maximum <n>' + 'mac-address sticky' + 'violation <mode>'.

questions.stem: A port-security violation put Gi0/3 into err-disabled. Which action restores it (after fixing the cause)?

options.text: 'shutdown' then 'no shutdown' on the interface (or configure errdisable recovery)

explanation.correct: An err-disabled port is recovered by bouncing it ('shutdown' then 'no shutdown') once the offending device is removed, or automatically via 'errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation' with a timer.

distractors.B: A full reload is unnecessary and disruptive.
distractors.C: Deleting the VLAN doesn't clear err-disable and breaks connectivity.
distractors.D: Speed changes don't recover an err-disabled port.

explanation.exam_pattern: Recover err-disable: fix cause → shut/no shut, or enable errdisable recovery. Default violation mode (shutdown) err-disables the port.

questions.stem: What does DHCP snooping insert into client DHCP requests (when option 82 is enabled) as they are relayed?

options.text: Option 82 (DHCP relay agent information) identifying the switch/port the request came from

explanation.correct: With option 82, DHCP snooping adds relay-agent information (circuit/remote ID = switch and port) to requests, which the server can use for assignment/policy and auditing of where a client connected.

distractors.B: No password is inserted.
distractors.C: OSPF LSAs are routing data, unrelated to DHCP.
distractors.D: BPDUs are STP messages, not DHCP option data.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP snooping + option 82 = relay-agent info (which switch/port). Builds the binding table that DAI/IP Source Guard rely on.

questions.stem: What threat does DHCP snooping primarily mitigate on untrusted access ports?

options.text: A rogue DHCP server handing out bad addresses/gateways (DHCP spoofing)

explanation.correct: DHCP snooping blocks DHCP server messages (OFFER/ACK) from untrusted ports, stopping a rogue DHCP server from assigning clients a malicious gateway/DNS (which would enable man-in-the-middle).

distractors.B: Route poisoning is a Layer 3 routing concern, not DHCP snooping's job.
distractors.C: BGP hijacking is an inter-domain routing issue.
distractors.D: STP loops are handled by spanning tree / BPDU Guard.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP snooping stops rogue DHCP servers (spoofing) on untrusted ports and builds the binding table for DAI/IPSG.

questions.stem: In IPsec, what does IKE Phase 1 establish?

options.text: A secure, authenticated management channel (ISAKMP SA) used to negotiate the data SAs
The actual encrypted data tunnel for user traffic
The DHCP lease for the tunnel

explanation.correct: IKE Phase 1 authenticates the peers and builds a secure ISAKMP/IKE SA — the protected channel used to negotiate the Phase 2 IPsec SAs that carry user data.

distractors.B: The data-carrying IPsec SAs are negotiated in Phase 2, over the Phase 1 channel.
distractors.C: IKE isn't a routing adjacency.
distractors.D: IKE doesn't assign DHCP leases for the tunnel.

explanation.exam_pattern: IKE Phase 1 = authenticate peers + build the IKE/ISAKMP SA. Phase 2 = negotiate the IPsec SAs (ESP/AH) that protect user data.

questions.stem: Why are GRE and IPsec often combined (GRE over IPsec) for site-to-site VPNs?

options.text: GRE carries multicast/routing protocols and multiple protocols; IPsec adds the encryption GRE lacks
IPsec carries routing protocols but can't encrypt
GRE encrypts and IPsec tunnels multicast

explanation.correct: Plain IPsec (tunnel mode) doesn't natively carry multicast/routing updates; GRE does, but offers no encryption. GRE-over-IPsec gives you both: run a routing protocol over the GRE tunnel and encrypt it with IPsec.

distractors.B: IPsec provides the encryption; it's GRE that carries multicast/multiproto.
distractors.C: Reversed — GRE tunnels (no crypto), IPsec encrypts.
distractors.D: GRE-over-IPsec is a very common combination.

explanation.exam_pattern: GRE = multiprotocol/multicast tunnel, no crypto. IPsec = encryption. GRE-over-IPsec = routed, encrypted site-to-site (DMVPN builds on this).

questions.stem: What does 'intent-based networking' (as with a central controller) mean?

options.text: Admins declare the desired business outcome/policy; the controller translates it into device configuration and verifies it
Each device is configured by hand via the CLI
The network chooses its own IP addresses randomly

explanation.correct: Intent-based networking is declarative: you express the intent (who can talk to whom, what policy), and the controller renders it into device configs, then uses assurance/telemetry to confirm the network matches the intent.

distractors.B: Hand CLI per device is the traditional imperative approach intent-based networking replaces.
distractors.C: It doesn't randomize addressing.
distractors.D: Routing still runs; intent sits above it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Declarative/intent = say WHAT you want; controller does HOW + verifies. Imperative = you specify each step/command.

questions.stem: On an SDN controller, which interface do business applications use to request network services or read state?

options.text: The northbound interface (NBI), typically a REST API

explanation.correct: Applications talk UP to the controller via the northbound interface (usually REST APIs) to express intent or query state. The controller talks DOWN to devices via southbound interfaces (NETCONF/OpenFlow).

distractors.B: The southbound interface faces the network devices, not the apps.
distractors.C: A console port is local device management, not the app interface.
distractors.D: A management VLAN is transport, not the programmatic API.

explanation.exam_pattern: Northbound = apps↔controller (REST). Southbound = controller↔devices (NETCONF/OpenFlow). Memorize the direction.

questions.stem: Which statement about RESTCONF is correct?

options.text: It uses HTTP(S) and REST verbs (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) with JSON or XML, over YANG models
It uses SSH on port 830 with XML-only RPCs
It is a CLI screen-scraping protocol

explanation.correct: RESTCONF exposes YANG-modeled data over HTTP(S) using standard REST verbs and JSON or XML encodings — a web-friendly alternative to NETCONF.

distractors.B: SSH/830 with XML RPCs describes NETCONF, not RESTCONF.
distractors.C: RESTCONF is a structured API over YANG, not screen scraping.
distractors.D: It doesn't use SNMP community strings.

explanation.exam_pattern: RESTCONF = HTTP(S) + REST verbs + JSON/XML (YANG). NETCONF = SSH 830 + XML RPC + datastores (YANG). Both model-driven.

questions.stem: Which NETCONF datastore represents the currently active, running configuration of a device?

explanation.correct: The 'running' datastore is the live, in-effect configuration. 'candidate' is an editable scratch copy you commit to running, and 'startup' is what loads at boot.

distractors.B: 'candidate' is a proposed config you validate then commit.
distractors.C: 'startup' is the saved boot config.
distractors.D: 'backup' is not a standard NETCONF datastore.

explanation.exam_pattern: NETCONF datastores: running (active), candidate (edit→commit), startup (boot). RESTCONF edits the running/intended data directly.
